15. In Article Nos. 27, 31 and 40 of the Constitution of Bangladesh vowed to guarantee equality before law, protection of law and right to profession or occupation for every citizen of Bangladesh in the following verses: —
"Equality before law
27. All citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law.
Right to protection of law
31. To enjoy the protection of the law, and to be treated in accordance with law, and only in accordance with law, is the inalienable right of every citizen, wherever he may be, and of every other person for the time being within Bangladesh, and in particular no action detrimental to the life, liberty, body, reputation or property of any person shall be taken except in accordance with law.
Freedom of profession or occupation 40. Subject to any restrictions imposed by law, every citizen possessing such qualifications, if any, as may be prescribed by law in relation to his profession, occupation, trade or business shall have the right to enter upon any lawful profession or occupation, and to conduct any lawful trade or business."
16. However, in the case of wretched Salil Kanti Chakrabarty we find that violating all of the aforementioned fundamental rights was not only denied but also mutilated by the state machineries concerned for a lifetime period of long 45 years till date. What he tried to do was to get admission in the Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) course in the Chittagong Medical College, a prestigious educational institution, course as well. Then as we have seen already that on the charges of doctoring with the mark sheets etc his selection was cancelled and after 21 years, however, he got acquitted from the accusations as the state failed to prove his guilt after another 10 elongated years. Maybe the writ petitioner thought that his miseries came to an end and he would be enrolled in his long cherished MBBS course. However, then the infamous red-tapism started to play its role. Mr Salil's case started to leap from one table to another like a Pingpong Ball and each of the government officials passed the Ball from his table to the others table like a champion Table Tennis player. Every one tried shifted their burden to others as good as possible and as expected, Mr Salil was not able to get admitted in the course albeit he left no stone unturned to achieve what was his fundamental right as enshrined in the Constitution.
17. We have gone through the judgment of the High Court Division and find that the bench studiously delved into the merit of the case, fateful journey of the writ petitioner and finally reached in a correct verdict.
18. We find no substance in all of the contentions raised by the learned Attorney-General for the appellants. Our considered view is that the High Court Division upon correct assessment of the materials on record and absolutely germane grounds arrived at a right and just decision. We, therefore, find no reasons to interfere with the same.
19. The facts of this case of ill-fated Salil Kanti Chakrabarty reminisce us a legendary dialogue by Indian Bangla acting Maestro of classical age, Chhabi Biswas in the movie named "Sobar Upore" (Beyond All). In the film the protagonist as acted by Chhabi Biswas was sentenced to life imprisonment for alleged murder of a lady whom he is accused of loving and then dumping and murdering heinously.
20. Twelve years later, his only son who became a lawyer, with the aid of some other protagonists secretly conjure up various evidences against the actual criminal, a government lawyer who originally fought the case against his father 12 years back. He gets the help of a journalist who, by his reports and friends in the Press, gathers public momentum to finally reopen the case. Then he presents the case himself and through various evidences and tact presentations, successfully pleads in favour of his father and proves thc involvement of the actual criminal, the government lawyer, who killed the lady to benefit from a huge insurance in her name. The accused was acquitted. Meanwhile, with 12 years of wretched life in the prisons and the thought that his wife and child had perished due to poverty, he seems to lose his mental balance. When the learned Judge pronounced the verdict of acquittal then the protagonist pronounced this celebrated dialogue.
21. In light of the facts of this case it is 45 years i.e. 3.5 times lengthy and the question should be asked- who will give back the lost 45 years of Mr Salil Kanti Chakrabarty? Or is it truly possible to return the most fruitful 45 years of life span of a young man who is now an aged man of 62 years? At the fag end of lifespan is it possible for him to study medical sciences for another five plus years and graduated after passing all the written, practical and viva-voce examinations? Practically speaking, Mr Salil's long cherished desire to become an MBBS Doctor gets in Bengali proverbial term "Salil Samadhi (ANzizi 44430" i.e. buried under the water. But, for what? What are his faults for getting such a fatal blow in his dream in such a cruel manner? There are no answers for these questions. It is the concerned government functionaries who are solely responsible for such a miscarriage of justice.
22. In the Preamble of our Constitution solemnly promised that: —
"... it shall be a fundamental aim of the State to realise through the democratic process a socialist society, free from exploitation a society in which the rule of law, fundamental human rights and freedom, equality and justice, political, economic and social, will be secured for all citizens;"
23. Then in the Article 7 it is firmly reiterated that—
"All powers in the Republic belong to the people this Constitution is, as the solemn expression of the will of the people, the supreme law of the Republic..."
24. If such is the situation, then state functionaries cannot go scot free after such type of harassment to a citizen of this land. The collective conscience of the nation must lift up and respond appropriately. As the Guardian of the Constitution, it is our duty to deliver justice as much as possible to an ill-treated son of this soil every centimeter of which country was soaked with the blood, toil and tears of the martyrs and heroic freedom fighters of 1971. Our considered view is that Mr Salil must be compensated financially by the state functionaries, though it would not bring back his golden days, however, it certainly establish that there is hope for the destitute and caution for the wrongdoers in this country. Here comes the key issue for our contemplation is whether in the exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 104, this Court can pass an order for the payment of money if such an order is in the form of compensation resulting upon the denial of a fundamental right.
25. Like ours, in the United States of America and in our nearest country India the parameters of State legal responsibility for its servants' tortious acts were not defined by legislation. However, the US Supreme Court has invoked the principles of human rights jurisprudence to compensate the victims of "governmental lawlessness" in the cases of James Monroe, et al. vs Frank Pape, et al. reported in 365 US 167 (1961). This decision created an avenue for individuals to argue that the Constitution itself regulated State government officials' acts. In addition it's not only provided for compensation to injured citizens infringements of constitutional rights, but greatly dissuaded capricious measures by government officials. Though the Supreme Court dismissed the case against the city itself, finding that Congress had not intended the word "person" in the law concerned to apply to municipalities. This aspect of Monroe was later partially overruled in Monell vs Department of Social Services of the City of New York, 436 US 658 (1978) which held that local governments were "persons" under the law and could face liability under certain circumstances.
26. In 1971, in the signpost case of Webster Bivens vs Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics reported in 403 US 388 (1971), the US Apex Court held that the violation of the Fourth Amendment of the Constitution could be made the basis of a civil suit against erring federal, officers. The US Constitution, through the Fourth Amendment, protects people from unreasonable searches and seizures by the government. The Bivens Ruling filled the remedial gap created after Monroe, for individuals wishing to bring suits for the misconduct of federal officials. Justice John Marshall Harlan II, in his famous statement, said: —
"For people in Bivens' shoes, it is damages or nothing. ... For the reasons set forth below, I am of the opinion that federal courts do have the power to award damages for violation of 'constitutionally protected interests' and I agree with the Court that a traditional judicial remedy such as damages is appropriate to the vindication of the personal interests protected by the Fourth Amendment."
27. In this way, it was decided by the US Apex Court that the American Bill of Rights is a constitutional restraint, commanding enough to be straightforwardly made the foundation of an action for damages, with no awaiting legislative endorsement.
28. In the Indian jurisdiction the break through was achieved in the case of Devaki Nandan Prasad vs State of Bihar and Others reported in AIR 1983 SC 1134. Here, the petitioner's pension had been delayed for twelve years. Without much discussion in the judgment, "exemplary costs" were awarded to the petitioner for "intentional, deliberate and motivated" harassment of the petitioner, though no specific rights violation was cited.
29. In the same year, the precedent-setting case of Rudul Sah vs State of Bihar and others was decided. Here the petitioner, who had been acquitted by the Court of Sessions, but not released from prison for fourteen years, presented a habeas corpus petition, wherein he also sought certain ancillary remedies like rehabilitation, reimbursement of expenses for medical treatment, and compensation for illegal incarceration. While disposing of the case of wretched Rudul Sah, the then Chief Justice of India YV Chandrachud's view is worth reading: —
"In these circumstances, the refusal of this Court to pass an order of compensation in favour of the petitioner will be doing mere lip-service to his fundamental right to liberty which the State Government has so grossly violated. Article 21 which guarantees the right to life and liberty will be denuded of its significant content if the power of this Court were limited to passing orders to release from illegal detention. One of the telling ways in which the violation of that right can reasonably be prevented and due compliance with the mandate of Article 21 secured, is to mulct its violaters in the payment of monetary compensation. Administrative sclerosis leading to flagrant infringements of fundamental rights cannot be corrected by any other method open to the judiciary to adopt."
His Lordship continues:—
"The right to compensation is some palliative for the unlawful acts of instrumentalities which act in the name of public interest and which present for their protection the powers of the State as a shield. If civilisation is not to perish in this country as it has perished in some others too well-known to suffer mention, it is necessary to educate ourselves into accepting that, respect for the rights of individuals is the true bastion of democracy. Therefore, the State must repair the damage done by its officers to the petitioner's rights. It may have recourse against those officers."
30. In the case of Railway Board vs Chandrima Das reported in 2 SCC 465, the Court mulled over the matter whether the High Court could entertain the petition filed by the respondent by way of public interest litigation and award compensation of Rs. 10 lakhs to Hanuffa Khatoon, a national of Bangladesh, who was sexually assaulted by the employees of the Eastern Railway. While rejecting the argument of the appellant that the victim of rape could have availed remedy by filling suit in a civil court, the Supreme Court of India observed:—
"Where public functionaries are involved and the matter relates to the violation of Fundamental Rights or the enforcement of public duties, the remedy would still be available under the public law notwithstanding that a suit could be filed for damages under private law. It was more so when it was not a mere matter of violation of an ordinary right of a person but the violation of fundamental rights which was Involved as petitioner was a victim of rape which is violative of the fundamental right of a person guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution."
31. In MC Mehta vs Union of India (AIR 1987 SC 1086], while dealing with a writ petition, filed for closure of certain units, the Supreme Court observed as follows:
"...The applications for compensation are for enforcement of the fundamental right to life enshrined in Art 21 of the Constitution and while dealing with such applications, a hyper-technical approach which would defeat the ends of justice could not be adopted. If the court is prepared to accept a letter complaining of violation of the fundamental right of an individual or a class of individuals who cannot approach the court for justice, there is no reason why the applications for compensation which have been made for enforcement of the fundamental right of the persons affected by the oleum gas leak under Article 21 should not be entertained. The Court while dealing with an application for enforcement of a fundamental right must look at the substance and not the forum".
32. The Court further observed:
"...We are also of the view that this Court under Article 32(1) is free to devise any procedure appropriate for the particular purpose of the proceeding, namely, enforcement of a fundamental right and under Article 32(2) has the implicit power to issue whatever direction, order or writ is necessary the Court in a given case, including all incidental or ancillary power necessary to secure enforcement of the fundamental right The power of the Court is not only injunctive in ambit, that is, preventing the infringement of a fundamental right, but it is also remedial in scope and provides relief against a breach of the fundamental right already committed vide Bandhua Mukti Morcha's case (supra). If the Court was powerless to issue any direction, order or writ in cases where a fundamental right has already been violated, Article 32 would be robbed of all its efficacy, because then the situation would be that if a fundamental right is threatened to be violated, the Court can injunct such violation but if the violator is quick enough to take action infringing the fundamental right, he would escape from the net of Article 32. That would, to a large extent, emasculate the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 32 and render it impotent and futile. We must, therefore, hold that Article 32 is not powerless to assist a person when he finds that his fundamental right has been violated. He can in that event seek remedial assistance under Article 32. The power of the Court to grant such remedial relief may include the power to award compensation in appropriate cases....The infringement of fundamental right must be gross and patent, that is, incontrovertible and ex-facie glaring and either such infringement should be on a large scale affecting the fundamental rights of a large number of persons,. or it should appear unjust or unduly harsh or oppressive on account of their poverty or disability or socially or economically disadvantaged position to require the person or persons affected by such infringement to initiate and pursue action in the civil courts. It is only in exceptional cases, compensation may be awarded in a petition under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution."
33. In Smt. Nilabati Behera vs State of Orissa reported in 1993 (2) SCC 746 the victim was arrested by the police, handcuffed and kept in police custody. His corpse was found on a train line the next day. The Court awarded compensation to the mother of the deceased on the subsequent grounds:—
"...Enforcement of the constitutional right and grant of redress embraces award of compensation as part of the legal consequences of its contravention....A claim in public law for compensation" for contravention of human rights and fundamental freedoms, the protection of which is guaranteed in the Constitution, is an acknowledged remedy for enforcement and protection of such rights, and such a claim based on strict liability made by resorting to a constitutional remedy provided for the enforcement of a fundamental right is "distinct from, and in additional to, the remedy in private law for damages for the tort' resulting from the contravention of the fundamental right. The defence of sovereign immunity being inapplicable and alien to the concept of guarantee of fundamental rights, there can be no question of such a defence being available in the constitutional remedy. It is this principle which justifies award of monetary compensation for contravention of fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, when that is the only practicable mode of redress available for the contravention made by - the state or its servants in the purported exercise of their powers, and enforcement of the fundamental right is claimed by resort to the remedy in public law under the Constitution by recourse to Articles 31 and 226 of the Constitution."
34. The Court further goes to observe that:—
"Therefore, when the court moulds the relief by granting "compensation" in proceedings under Article 32 or 226 of the Constitution seeking enforcement or protection of fundamental rights, it does so under the public law by way of penalizing the wrongdoer and fixing the liability of the public wrong on the State which has failed in its public duty to protect the fundamental rights of the citizen. The payment of compensation in such cases is not to be understood, as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the private law but in the broader sense of providing relief by an order of making 'monetary amends' under the public law for the wrong done due to breach of public duty, of not protecting the fundamental rights of the citizen. The compensation is in the nature of 'exemplary damages' awarded against the wrongdoer for the breach of its public law duty and is independent of the rights available to the aggrieved party to claim compensation under the private law in an action based on tort, through a suit instituted in a court of competent jurisdiction or/and prosecute the offender under the penal law."
35. In UP State Co-operative Land Development Bank Ltd. vs Chandra Bhyan Dubey reported in 1999 (1) SCC 741 it was observed that:—
"The Constitution is not a statute. It is a fountainhead of all the statutes....When any citizen or person is wronged the High Court will step in to protect him, be that wrong be done by the State, or an instrumentality of the State...."
36. In the case of DK Basu vs State (1997) 1 SCC 416, it has also been observed:—
"A court of law cannot close its consciousness and aliveness to stark realities. Mere punishment of the offender cannot give much solace to the family of the victim-civil action for damages are a long-drawn and a cumbersome judicial process. Monetary compensation for redressal by the court is, therefore, useful and at times perhaps the only effective remedy to apply balm to the wounds of the family members of the deceased victim, who may have been the breadwinner of the family. "
37. Basing on the aforementioned pondering and verdicts, it is obvious that even if there is no articulated stipulation in the Constitution of India for yielding of compensation to the sufferers by the State for the encroachment of their right to life and individual autonomy assured by the Article 21 (which is equivalent to Article 32 of our Constitution concerning protection of right to life
and personal liberty) of the Constitution of India, nonetheless the Indian Apex Court has judicially advanced that such victims are entitled to get reimbursement under public law besides the remedies obtainable surrounded by private law.
38. To meet this end, our Apex. Court has already set forth the beginning point of the evolution of the concept of "Constitutional Tort" in our jurisdiction in the case of Government of Bangladesh and Others vs Children's Charity Bangladesh Foundation (CCB Foundation) and Others (famously called as Child Jihad's Case) reported in LEX/BDAD/0023/2018. In the original case of Children's Charity Bangladesh Foundation (CCB Foundation) vs Bangladesh and Others reported in 2018 13 ALR (HCD) 45 [Writ Petition No. 12388 of 2014] the High Court Division awarded BDT 20 Lac  as monetary compensation within 90 (ninety) days from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment and order to be paid by the State owned agencies Bangladesh Railway and the Directorate of Fire Service and Civil Defense equally to the parents of unfortunate child Jihad for their inaction, negligence, failure in respect of rescuing the minor boy of 4(four) years which resulted in his tragic and shocking death. High Court Division further ordered that the order of awarding compensation will not impede/affect other liabilities, if there be any, of the respondents concern or its officials resulting from the death of the said victim.
39. Thereafter, two appeals were filed against the said judgment and order of the High Court Division one of it was from the Government of Bangladesh and while dismissing both of the appeals this Appeal this Division affirmed the judgment and order of the High Court Division in toto by stating that:—
"Considering the facts and circumstances of the cases, we find no legal infirmity in the impugned judgment factually and legally calling for interference by this Court. Accordingly, we find no merit in these petitions and the same are dismissed."
40. The case in brief is that a 4 years aged boy named Zihad, while playing in the Shahjahanpur Railway Colony playground located at the capital city of Dhaka fell inside the 16 inches uncovered shaft which was left dumped by Bangladesh Railway and WASA authorities. The said awful occurrence took place at 3-30 pm on 26-12-2014 which was lively aired and published all the way through all electronic and print media of the country. However, the after long 10-12 hours unsuccessful rescue operation by the Bangladesh Railway and the Directorate of Fire Service and Civil Defense left the place of occurrence wrapping up their operation. But a few volunteers by using their hand-made apparatus pulled up the dead body of. Jihad from within a short time after it was declared by the respondents concern that there was nothing in the pipe, parting the entire country perturbed, tight-lipped and traumatized.
41. Prior to that a division Bench of the High Court Division in the case of ZI Khan Panna vs Bangladesh reported in LEX/BDHC/0170/2015 (Writ Petition No.7650 of 2012, decided On: 13-9-2015) first formulated the legal basis of "Constitutional. Tort" as adopted wholly in the above mentioned case of Jihad decided by the Division Bench of High Court Division. In the case of ZI Khan Panna vs Bangladesh the constitutional validity of Joint Actions Immunity Act,' 2003 (CAN RiasIS Wrfrift Rirkw, .k000) promulgated on 9th January, 2003 providing for the indemnity of all disciplined forces and Government officials for the detention, arrest, search, interrogation and such other actions taken against the citizens between 16th October, 2002 and 9th January, 2003 pursuant to the order dated 16th October, 2002 and other subsequent orders of the Government. During the said period concerned disciplined forces and Government functionaries were authored to conduct drives under the name and style 'Operation Clean Heart' all over the country as and when required and accordingly they conducted drives till 9th January, 2003. In the newspaper reports it was alleged that during the 'Operation Clean Heart', at least 43 (forty-three) people were killed and hundreds were injured in the custody of the Joint Forces. Compensation was sought for the victims of torture and of custodial deaths, the dependants/ family members of the deceased under constitutional scheme.
42. The command to evolve this mode of Constitutional compensation may be derived directly from the language and purpose of Article 102 itself. Further, the court will be unable to effectively fulfill its role of protector and guarantor of the citizens' indefensible rights, if it leaves those aggrieved of fundamental rights infringements, to seek civil remedies.
43. Appellate Division in Bangladesh vs Nurul Amin reported in 67 DLR (AD) 352 observed that:—
"We have no hesitation in holding that the paramount object and purpose for which Article 102 has been enacted and the relevant factor and provision on which the interpretation of the Article 102 has been linked, the High Court Division in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution, which is an instrumentality and a mechanism, containing both substantive and procedural provisions "to realise the objectives, purposes, policies, rights and duties which [the people] have set out for themselves and which they have strewn over the fabric of the Constitution," can award monetary compensation or compensatory cost mostly in appropriate cases for violation of fundamental rights which must be gross and patent i.e. incontrovertible and ex facie glaring or that violation should appear unjust, unduly harsh or oppressive on account of the victim's disability or personal circumstance ....That is why the Court has to act firmly but with certain amount of circumspection and self-restraint, lest proceedings under Article 102 are misused as "appropriate cases" or "a disguised substitute for civil action in private law" It is only in the exceptional cases of the nature indicated above that compensation or compensatory cost may be awarded to a victim in a petition properly drawn under Article 102 of the Constitution. The violation must be gross and its magnitude must be such as "to shock the conscience of the Court" and it would be gravely unjust to the person whose fundamental right was violated to require him to go to the Civil Court for claiming compensation."
44. In the case of Habihullah Khan vs Azaharuddin, 35 DLR (AD) 72 this Division observed that:—
"...awarding of compensatory costs is no doubt a matter of discretion of the Court, but it must be exercised judiciously."
45. As such our considered reiteration is that Constitutional compensation for any victim of lawlessness of any government functionary is a Constitutional mandate.
46. If it is so, then approaches the next issues as to the determinations and assessments of quantum of compensation, finding out the "appropriate cases" for awarding compensation, personal versus state liability etc.
47. Indian Supreme Court in Rudul Sah's case, held that writ compensation will be awarded only in "cases of gross violation." In Nilabati Behera's case some principles in assessing the amount of compensation such as, the age of the victim; their last and potential earning capacity were laid down. However, there should not be any hard and fast rule for assessment of compensations, the calculation ought to be made on a fact specific basis, and its application to all situations, may not be feasible. Quantum of compensation must essentially differ, depending upon the gravity and surrounding circumstances of the rights violation, the possibility of mala fides on the part of the concerned official, the extent of the disregard shown towards the possible infringement of the right, the loss of life or limb, the number and condition of any dependants of the victim, her/his earning capacity, and the need to send out a clear signal to the administration, that callousness towards citizens' rights will not be countenanced. In appropriate cases, courts have to award compensation as an interim measure, and have left the remedy to approach the civil court to claim damages open to the aggrieved persons. The only sine qua non that could be imposed, in our opinion is, judicial decisions on this point must be backed by consistent reasoning as far as is possible.
48. It has been observed by the predecessor of this Division in the case of Sri Manmath Nath Kiwi vs Mvi. Md Mokhlesur Rahman reported in 22 DLR (SC) 51 that:—
"Assessment of damages in such a case must, therefore, necessarily be to some extent of a rough and approximate nature based more or less on guess work, for, it may will be impossible to accurately determine the loss which has been sustained by the death of a husband, wife, parent or child."
49. Concerning the lawlessness of the government officials, the widely accepted view is that State liability is the natural choice, as opposed to personal liability, since it ensures effective compensation for the victim. Further, avoidance of over-deterring conscientious officers from taking decisions that are in the public interest, is also a factor. Large amounts of discretion are vested in administrative officers, and they cannot perform their functions if their hands are constrained by invisible chains. There is, however, must be some exception if situation arises. In Rudul Sah and Saheli (Saheli, A Women's Resources Centre, through MS Nalini Bhanot vs Commissioner of Police, Delhi 1990 AIR 513) cases, the Court opined that the State might proceed against the deviant officer. In certain other cases, the court has directly held the deviant officers personally liable. It is further usually accepted that when the court awards compensation, it is at the end of the day the taxpayer's money which is being spent to make up for inaction or wrongful action, on the part of government officials, and in such cases, though immediate payment should be made from the public funds, the same should be recovered from the errant officers/functionaries.
50. The pain, anguish, mental agony, physical incapability, emotion and price of relentless fighting spirit are not humanly computable. We are contented that the respondent is entitled to any compensation that can be only in lump sum and not on itinerary of calculation.
51. In our case, what we witnessed is that one ominous morning the young aged respondent who was selected for being admitted in a public medical college informed that his selection was cancelled on allegation of doctoring in the mark sheets. A simple intimation from the concerned Education Board concerning the veracity of said mark sheets could certainly end all of the controversies. However, find no such attempts from the concerned state functionaries, rather observed that all of the state machineries like Principal of the Medical College, Admission Committee, Directorate of Health, different ministries of the government, Anti-corruption Bureau, Superintendent of Police of Bandarban and many more, stand against a helpless young lad of religious and ethnic minority from a backward hilly region of the country. Being harassed by them for 21 years, the ill-fated admission seeker was booked by a criminal case from where he had to fight against whole world for 15 years more to get acquitted. However, he was unsuccessful in getting admission albeit no stone unturned and knocking multiple times at every door concerned and finally the concerned State Minister's recommendation too was turned as a failure. Thereafter, for the last 16 years he is fighting the ultimate legal dragging his dream in the Apex court of the land. In this elongated warfare for justice, we amazingly observed that the ambidextrous soldier of one man army is still standing and fighting like a indomitable warrior sworn in not to recede. This Myrmidon is worthy of paying a salute. At the same time, a deep sigh should be breathed thinking that if this unstoppable spirit was allowed to become an MBBS doctor, he would certainly carry this superb passion, zeal, dedication and unconquerable fighting spirit in his 'would be' professional journey. If so, he could serve millions of people and accomplish seine ultimate personal achievements and/or national pride. No one can foretell the future, but, we can assume the probability basing on some existing facts and flaming patterns. These 'near probable' loss of an individual is irreparable and of the community, of the nation are beyond one's mind's eye. Hundreds of Crore will not be enough for compensating this dejected soul.
52. In the original writ petition, the writ petitioner-respondent here, although not file the writ petition for compensation, rather, for admission in MBBS course. After the long legal fight, now he is aged of 62 years. At this juncture, we are of the considered view that, there is no legal infirmity and illegality in the judgment of the High Court Division for interference by this Division. It is, therefore, obvious that, the appeal should be dismissed. Now core question to us after dismissal of appeal is it possible on the respondent-writ petitioner to study MBBS at the age of 62 years on getting admission in the 1st year in the Chattogram Medical College, it would not possible on the part of the writ petitioner-respondent here at age of 62 years to complete his study, if now he got admission by the order of the Court, but, it was possible on his part, when he was acquitted from the criminal case, but, the appellants failed to get admission.
53. At the hearing of the appeal, the learned Attorney-General strongly pointed out that, although appeal was filed by some of the writ respondents, but, the Government machineries once again directed the Principal, Chattogram Medical College for admission of the writ petitioner even before filing the writ petition and after judgment of the High Court Division, so, according to the learned Attorney-General, the failure of the Principal of the Chattogram Medical College may not be shifted to the shoulders of all the respondents. We have carefully perused the whole records and connected papers and consider the submissions of the learned Attorney-General. So, from the whole case it appears that, the Principal of the Chattogram Medical College was actually responsible to admit the writ petitioner who did not care to take steps to admit the writ petitioner-respondent in MBBS course nor take any legal steps against the judgment of the High Court Division.
54. From the above discussions and facts and circumstances, we have no option, but, to take legal and lawful course of action against the writ respondent No.4, Principal, Chattogram Medical College, Chattogram i.e. the Principals who were acted as Principal from the session 1978-79 to today for non-compliance of the Court's order. Although, this Division stayed the operation of the judgment and order dated 1-8-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.4243 of 2005, but, all the then. Principals of the Chattogram Medical College worked from the Sessions 1978-79 till today by virtue of their negligence and illegal activities committed serious disobedient to the judgment and order of the High Court Division. The principals from the sessions 1978-79 to onward till today/were/are liable for non-compliance of the order of the High Court Division as well as in violation the orders of the Health Directorate and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare by not acting according to their suggestions and orders.
55. In view of the above scenarios, we are of the considered view that, the writ respondent Nos. 1-3 as petitioner Nos.1-3 herein were not solely responsible for not to admitting the writ petitioner-respondent herein, rather, it is clearly apparent on the face of the record that, all the Principals from the Session 1978-79 of the Chattogram Medical College, Chattogram onward to today are absolutely liable for non-compliance of the order of the Government passed by the appropriate authority and lastly, judgment and order of the High Court Division. Therefore, all the principals are equally liable.
<u>56. In our view, this is an exceptional case with exceptional scenario, though we are agreeing to dismiss this appeal. However, it is not possible on the part of the writ petitioner respondent herein, now to admit in the Chattogram Medical College, Chattogram for MBBS study. Since, the writ petitioner-respondent herein, was fighting for a period of 37 years for establishing his fundamental right and legal remedy. But, today in fact, we cannot compel the writ petitioner-respondent herein, to study MBBS course in the Chattogram Medical College, Chattogram. But, question is, what is legal remedy for the writ petitioner-respondent herein, in accordance with the Constitution of the Bangladesh. To establish the fundamental right, the writ petitioner-respondent herein lost his valuable and golden time of his life, not only that, but, he has suffered a lots with mental disturb and agony. His offspring has also suffered a lot due to his failure to study the MBBS and become a Doctor, he has further suffered from social status and Justice. Since the writ petitioner-respondent herein tried to establish his fundamental right from the year 1976-78 sessions. We cannot shut our eyes as Constitution given us mandate to give remedy the writ petitioner-respondent herein in the form of complete justice. Therefore, we are of the pious view and opinion that, it is the fit case to apply the provision under of Article 104 of the Constitution to do complete justice, the words doing complete justice as occur in the aforementioned article are great significance. Their importance cannot be whittled down, nor can the Court give up even a fraction of this power. It is a great power with which the Court has been armed as decided this Division in the case of Mahbubur Rahman Sikder vs Mujibur Rahman Sikder, reported in 37 DLR (AD) 145. It has been further held by this Division to the effect that, "No remedy is available to the appellant though a gross injustice has been done to him for no fault or laches of his own", as decided by this Division in the case of Raziul Hasan vs Badiuzzaman Khan and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 71. We are, therefore, of the view that, to doing complete justice, this Division is hot prevented to give damage in mandatory term instead of direction to implement the Courts order.</u>
<u>57. Accordingly, instead of directing to admit the writ petitioner as respondent herein to the Chattogram Medical College, Chattorgram from the current sessions, we decide that, the writ respondent No.4, Principals of the Chattogram Medical College, Chattogram who were in the post of Principal from 1978-79 session to today all are to pay the loss and damage of the writ petitioner as respondent herein. Since there is no hard and fast rule to calculate the compensation under the Article 104 of the Constitution for suffering of the writ petitioner-respondent. He will be compensated at the tune of loss and sufferings.</u>
58. However, for being logical we must fix an amount and in our conscientious estimation, BDT 2,00,00,000 (Two crore) would be least amount coherent with the grave injustice done-by the government functionaries to the respondent.
<u>59. In the instant case, our considered view is that for ensuring complete justice, effective and speedy disbursement of compensatory amount awarded, the amount should be paid by the government first. Well, if the government thinks that taxpayer's money should not be wasted for the wrongdoing of some delinquent in service or retired state functionaries, after disbursing the total amount to the respondent or if that situation emerges to his heirs, government is at liberty in extracting the same amount from such delinquent state functionaries in accordance with laws after conducting an enquiry for determining the extent of liabilities of each and every Principals involved. The State must guarantee that there shall be no more Salil Kanti Chakrabarty in this Country. Otherwise, the basic props of society and caravan of human's advancement would be halted and fall apart.</u>
Accordingly, this appeal is dismissed. The writ respondent No.4, Principal(s) of the Chattogram Medical College, Chattogram from the session 1978-79 to today are directed to pay the aforesaid amount of Taka 200,00,000 (Taka two crore) within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of this judgment. The office is directed to serve a copy of this judgment to the present Principal of the Chattogram Medical College, Chattogram forthwith. The present Principal of the Chattogram Medical College, Chattogram is further directed to take necessary steps to pay the damage and compensation as directed by this Court in accordance with law.
End.

full_judgment:
The instant revision has been argued with great ability by the learned Advocates of both sides. As a result of their arguments on question of facts and law, the issue involved in the Rule has been narrowed down to a very short compass as to the admissibility of documentary evidence. 

2. The learned Assistant Judge, Mirsharai Sadar, Chattogram allowed the Other Suit No. 49 of 2005 on 28-3-2010. Decree was drawn on 1-4-2010. Other Appeal No. 97 of 2017 (former 201 of 2010) was dismissed on 18-10-2018 by the Special District Judge, Chattogram, Challenging the same the defendants filed the instant revision and obtained Rule on 8-4-2019. 

3. Plaintiff-opposite party Nos. 1, 3 and 4 entered appearance in the Rule. 

4. The plaint was amended two times before commencement of the trial. The plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in 15 decimals of land recorded in RS Khatian No. 3241, RS Plot No. 5239 corresponding to BS Khatian No. 1125, BS Plot Nos. 5919 and 5920. The plaintiffs further prayed for declaration that the registered sale deed Nos. 2229 dated 3-5-1960, 2508 dated 4-4-1987 and 116, 117 both dated 11-2-2005 and Mutation Case No. 54/88-89 are illegal and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs also prayed for a permanent injunction. 

5. The plaintiffs' case is that Abdul Kader was the owner of 22.5 decimals of land recorded in RS. Plot No. 5239. By a registered deed of gift No. 2329 dated 1-6-1946 (Exhibit. 3), he gifted the said 22.5 decimals of lands and other lands to his two daughters, namely Rowshan Banu and Hosne Banu in equal share. Rowshan Banu died leaving a daughter and a son who inherited her share in the lands. By a registered sale deed No. 3371 dated 27-4-1974 (Exhibit. 5), the heirs of Rowshan Banu sold the suit land consisting of 15 decimals, which was recorded in RS Plot No. 5239, to Abul Hossain. Hosne Banu by a registered sale deed No. 3083 dated 11-6-1974 (Exhibit. 4) sold lands including the land recorded in the RS Khatian No. 5239 to Abul Hossain. Thus, Abul Hossain became the owner of the lands including the suit land. The plaintiffs purchased the suit land from Abul Hossain by a registered deed No. 1698 dated 7-5-1987 (Exhibit. 7). Precisely, this is the chain of title of the plaintiffs. 

6. The contesting defendants admitted that Abdul Kader was the owner of 22.5 decimals of land. They denied the execution of the gift deed dated 1-6-1946 (Exhibit. 3) by Abdul Kader and subsequent execution of the sale deed dated 11-6-1974 (Exhibit. 4) and another sale deed dated 7-5-1987 (Exhibit. 7). Their specific case is that Abdul Kader kept the said 22.5 decimals of land in mortgage to one Munshi Mia in 1956. Munshi Mia was in possession of the land till 1960 as mortgagee. Abdul Kader could not redeem the mortgage. He was in need of money. Thereafter, by a registered sale deed No. 2229 dated 3-5-1960 (Exhibit. Kha) Abdul Kader sold 153/4 decimals of land out of 22.5 decimals to Munshi Mia's wife Ayesha Khatun. Thereafter, Ayesha Khatun sold the said 153/4 decimals of land (suit land) to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and to their brother Moazzem (since deceased). After purchase, they mutated the land in their names, vide Mutation Case No. 54/88-89. Thereafter, the defendants sold part of the suit land to other defendants. 

7. As noted earlier, the suit was decreed in favour of the plaintiff by the trial Court and the appellate Court below. Mr. Md. Omar Farook, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioners, submits that the foundation of the chain of title of the plaintiffs is the registered gift deed dated 1-6-1946 (Exhibit. 3). At the time of tendering the certified copy of the said gift deed in evidence by the PW-1 the defendants raised objection which is noted in the deposition sheet as well as on the back page of Exhibit-3. As such, the gift deed (Exhibit. 3) was inadmissible evidence as per provisions of the Evidence Act. However, both the Courts below did not consider this aspect of the case and decreed the suit treating Exhibit-3 as admissible evidence.  

8. The next argument of Mr. Omar Farook is that the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit land. On question of possession the trial Court relied on the oral evidence of the PWs and disbelieved the testimony of DWs and held that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land. The appellate Court below came to the same conclusion. Mr. Farook argued that both the Courts below did not at all consider the BS Khatian, rent receipts, mutation case proceedings tendered in evidence by the defendants in support of proof of possession of the suit land by them. The final argument of Mr. Farook is that the suit is barred by limitation. 

9. In reply, Mr. Sk. Md. Morshed, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite parties, submits that the defendants in their pleading did not deny the execution of the registered gift deed dated 1-6-1946 (Exhibit. 3). As such, as per provision of Order VIII rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) read with section 58 and clause (b) of section 65 of the Evidence Act, the certified copy of Exhibit-3 is admissible evidence. On question of possession and limitation, Mr. Morshed submits that both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land and that the suit is not barred by limitation. 

10. The point raised by Mr. Farook that Exhibit-3, which is the certified copy of the registered gift deed dated 1-6-1946 tendered in evidence by PW-1, is inadmissible is taken up first. 

11. Exhibit-3 is the foundation of the plaintiffs' case. It is noted that the defendants also raised objection as to admissibility of certified copies of sale deed dated 27-4-1974 (Exhibit. 5) and sale deed dated 7-5-1987 (Exhibit. 7) in evidence which also form part of the chain of title of the plaintiffs. The objections are recorded in the deposition sheet as well as on the back page of the Exhibited documents. 

12. The contents of documents may be proved either by primary or by secondary evidence (section 61 of Evidence Act). Section 62 provides that primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court. Under clause (l) of section 63 certified copies given under the provisions of section 65 are included as secondary evidence. Section 64 states that documents must be proved by primary evidence except in the cases mentioned in other provisions of the Evidence Act. Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given are set out in section 65. The relevant provisions of section 65 are reproduced below, 
"65. Secondary evidence may be given of the existence, condition or contents of a document in the following cases:- 
(a) -----------  
(b) when the existence, condition or contents of the original have been proved to be admitted in writing by the person against whom it is proved or by his representative in interest; 
(c)   -----------  
(d)   -----------  
(e) when the original is a. public document within the meaning of section 74; 
(f) -----------     
(g)  -----------   
In cases (a), (c), and (d) In case (b), the written admission is admissible. 
In case (e) or (f), a certified copy of the document, but no other kind of secondary evidence, is admissible. 
In case (g) ". 

13. When a certified copy of a document is tendered in evidence the same is subject to a large number of limitations. In H. Siddiqui vs A. Rattralingant, (2011) 4 SCC 240 it is held: 
"The provisions of section 65 of the 1872 Act provide for permitting the parties to adduce secondary evidence. However, such a course is subject to a large number of limitations. In a case where the orieinal documents are not produced at any time, nor has any factual foundation. laid for giving secondary evidence, it is not permissible for the court to allow a party to adduce secondary evidence. Thus, secondary evidence relating to the contents of a document is inadmissible, until the non-production of the original is accounted for, so as to bring it within one or other of the cases provided for in the section. The secondary evidence must be, authenticated by foundational evidence that the alleged copy is in fact a true copy of the original. Mere admission of a document in evidence does not amount to its proof. Therefore, the documentary evidence is required to be proved in accordance with law. The court has an obligation to decide the question of admissibility of a document in secondary evidence before making endorsement thereon". 

14. In the above-mentioned reported case, the photocopy of the power of attorney was shown to the respondent in his cross-examination and he admitted his signature. The Indian Supreme Court held that the respondent had merely admitted his signature on the photocopy of the power of attorney and did not admit the contents thereof. Admissibility of a document or contents thereof may not necessarily lead to drawing any inference unless the contents thereof have some probative value. 

15. In Abani Mohan Sana vs Assistant Custodian Vested Property, Chandpur and others, 39 DLR (AD) 223 the plaintiff's case was based on a registered gift deed. He tendered in evidence the certified copy of the said deed as Exhibit-1. In cross-examination, the plaintiff deposed that the original gift deed was burnt. He admitted that his house was not burnt. PW 2, who was the scribe, was the only other witness who stated that the executants signed the deed after it was written by him. The Apex Court observed that the evidence of PW 2 cannot by itself prove the genuineness of the gift deed. It was held by majority (4:1): 
"In the present case the plaintiff is claiming his title to the suit land on the basis of a deed of gift. I have got no doubt in my mind that the initial onus was on him to prove his title. The observation made in 32 DLR (AD) 29 would be of no avail to the appellant, as he failed to discharge his initial onus by proving his document of title. Had he succeeded to do so then the onus would have shifted on the Enemy Property Authority to prove that the executants of the plaintiff's document, the sons of Surendra Mohan Saha, were residing in an enemy country at the relevant time". 

16. Under section 79 of the Evidence Act, a Court is bound to draw the presumption that a certified copy of a document is genuine and also that the concerned officer signed it in the official character which he claimed in the said document. But such a presumption is permissible only if the certified copy is substantially in the form and purported to be executed in the manner provided by law in that manner. In other words, if the certified copy is executed substantially in the form and in the manner provided by the law, the Court raises a rebuttable presumption in regard to its genuineness. The scope of section 79 was considered in Bhinka and others vs Charm Singh, AIR 1959 SC 960. In this case, three Courts rejected the certified copy of the record-of-rights on the ground that it was not genuine on the basis of not only the internal evidence furnished by the document but also on other evidence. In this case, neither the official diary of the Patwary, who was the authorised officer to issue certified copies of the record-of-rights, was produced before the Court to prove that the prescribed procedure was followed nor the extract noted in the diary to disclose that the Patwary made any note of payment as required by law. The Indian Supreme Court held that it cannot, therefore, be said that the certified copy was issued by the Patwary in substantial compliance with the provisions of law governing such issue. It follows that the Court is not bound to draw the presumption in regard to its genuineness. It was further held that even if there was any rebuttable presumption, it was so rebutted. 

17. In the instant case, the plaintiffs neither called the concerned officer who issued the certified copies of Exhibit Nos. 3, 5 and 7 nor took steps to prove that those Exhibits are substantially in the form and purported to be executed in the manner directed by law in that behalf. Without taking such steps, the Court is not bound to draw the presumption of genuineness of Exhibit Nos. 3, 5 and 7 under section 79 of the Evidence Act when the other side raised objection as to their admissibility at the time of tendering those in evidence. 

18. In Soya Rani Guha alias Soya Rani Gupta vs Abdul Awal Mia and others, 47 DLR (AD) 45, the certified copy of the kabala was Exhibited without any objection. An explanation was given for non-production of the original kabala. It was held: 
"A registered sale deed is the primary evidence of the interest sold. Under section 74(2) of the Evidence Act, 1882 public record of a private document like a sale deed when kept in the office of the Sub-Registrar to which the public generally have access falls within the category of public document and .a certified copy. of such a document can be adduced as a secondary evidence, though the reception of such evidence will be of a weak character in place of the registered document evidencing the sale. 
Where a case for the reception of secondary evidence is made out under the provisions of section 65, a certified copy of a registered document becomes admissible in proof of the existence, condition and contents of the original document under the provision of section 57 (5) of the Registration Act, but the contents of the documents may not be conclusive evidence. 
The production of a certified copy of a sale deed does not, however, warrant the presumption of due execution of the original document. A party producing secondary evidence of a document is not relieved of the duty of proving the execution of the original. Even in a case where a document is Exhibited without objection the Court is to be satisfied as to the execution of the document". 

19. In Dr. Md. Forman Ali Miah vs Nizamuddin, 12 LM (AD) 138 no objection was raised at the time of proving Exhibit-Kha by producing the certified copy. It was held that when the original is a public document under section 74 of the Evidence Act and the original is a document of which a certified copy is permitted by the Act or by any other law in force in Bangladesh to be given in evidence the same may be given/filed in a Court and unless any objection is raised to such document when the same is filed it is very much admissible in evidence. 41 DLR (AD) 97 was followd and relied upon in Dr. Md. Forman All Miah. 

20. The above case laws unequivocally suggest that when a party to the proceedings desires to prove a document, he can do so by producing the certified copy of the original document by laying the factual foundation for giving secondary evidence as per provisions of section 65. Complication arises when the other side raises objection as to admissibility of the certified copy in evidence. Once objection is raised the party adducing the secondary evidence has no option but to follow and satisfy the requirements of the Evidence Act for admissibility of such secondary evidence. 

21. Against the backdrop of the factual matrix of the instant case, the proposition of law can be looked into from a different procedural perspective. Order XIII, rule 3 of the CPC empowers the trial Court to reject any document at any stage of the suit which it considers irrelevant or otherwise inadmissible even after admission of the document (Kissen vs Ram, 12 WR 13). When a document is marked as Exhibit without objection, the admissibility of the same cannot be challenged at appellate stage or subsequent stage (44 DLR (AD) 162, 12 LM (AD) 138. (2004) 7 SCC 107]. The rationale behind the principle is that objection as to the mode of proof falls within the procedural law. Therefore, such objections could be waived. The rule of fair play envisages that an objection, if taken at the appropriate point of time, would enable the party tendering the secondary evidence to cure the defect and resort to such mode of proof as would be regular. The omission to object becomes fatal because by his failure the party entitled to object allows the party tendering the secondary evidence to act on an assumption that the opposite party is not serious about the mode of proof ((2004) 7 SCC 107]. In the case in hand, in spite of objection raised by the defendants at the time of tendering Exhibit Nos. 3, 5 and 7 in evidence by the plaintiffs, which are certified copies of gift deed and sale deeds forming essential part of the chain of title of plaintiffs, they did not take steps to prove those documents in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law. Failure of the plaintiffs to prove documents (Exhibit. 3, 5 and 7) in accordance with law in the face of objection goes to the root of the matter regarding admissibility. Regrettably, the trial Court admitted those Exhibits in evidence and passed the decree based on those in violation of the law. 

22. Mr. Morshed appearing for the plaintiff-opposite parties refers to Exhibit-Ga series which are the attested copies of Union Parishad arbitration proceedings dated 11-1-1989 and Exhibit-Gha and Gha (1) which are certified copies of Mutation Case No. 54/88-89 and mutation proposal case No. 23/88-89 giving rise to the mutation case and submits that transfer of the suit land by Exhibit-3 had always been admitted by the defendants and as such, Exhibit-3 is not required to be proved under section 58 (facts admitted need not be proved) and clause (b) of section 65 of the Evidence Act. Exhibit-Ga series and Exhibit-Gha and Gha (1) were tendered in evidence by the defendants. Exhibit-Ga series are the photocopies of handwritten documents attested by the Union Parishad Chairman pertaining to an award given in a local salish conducted by the local Union Parishad Chairman. The award has no legal force. The admissibility of Exhibit-Ga series in evidence is highly questionable. In any event, it cannot be considered as admission of the defendants as to the deed gift dated 1-4-1946 (Exhibit. 3). The said gift deed has not been mentioned in. Exhibit-Gha (order dated 19-2-1989 passed by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) in Mutation Case No. 54/88-89). However, in Exhibit-Gha(1) (report of the concerned Tahsildar dated 24-1-1989 in Mutation Proposal Case No. 23/88-89), the gift deed of 1946 (Exhibit. 3) as well as the mortgage of the suit land in favour of Munshi Mia by Abdul Kader in 1956 and subsequent sale of the same to Munshi Mia's wife Ayesha Khatun by Abdul Kader which is the defendants' case, were mentioned. It is stated in Exhibit-Gha(1), "আবুল হোসেন (predecessor-in-interest of plaintiffs) তাহার ভগ্নি হইতে খরিদ করিয়া দখল পাওয়ার জন্য মুন্সি মিঞার বিরুদ্ধে থানাতে এক মামলা দায়ের করিলে বাদি ও বিবাদির মনোনিত ব্যক্তিদেরকে সালিস ১১-৯-৭৯ তারিখে নিয়োগ করিলে উভয় পক্ষের কাগজপত্র দেখিয়া আব্দুল কাদেরের শঠতা দেখিয়া মুন্সি মিঞার দখল বহাল রাখেন". The statements made in Exhibit-Gha(1) negates the contention of Mr. Morshed. 

23. Mr. Morshed argued that the defendants in their pleading did not categorically deny the plaintiffs' chain of title which is essentially linked to Exhibit-3. rather admitted in paragraph 20 of the written statement that ফলে বাদীগণের কোনরূপ স্বত্ব থাকিয়া থাকিলেও তাহা তামাদিতে বারিত হইয়া সকল স্বত্ত্ব বিলোপ হইয়াছে and, as such, Exhibit-3 is admissible evidence.

24. Mr. Farook, appearing for the defendant-petitioners, submits that the statement in question implies the alternative case of the defendants that if there be any title of the plaintiffs the same has been barred by limitation. Mr. Farook submits that the statement does not tantamount to admission of the plaintiffs' case. Mr. Morshed, on the other hand, submits that the pleading of the defendants being evasive and not being specific in stating the real facts starting from paragraph 18 of the written statements, the plaintiffs' case is admitted by operation of law. In this regard, I note that the defendants in paragraph No. 11 of their written statement categorically denied the plaintiffs' chain of title including the gift deed dated 1-6-1946 (Exhibit. 3) by stating,— 
"...রৌশন বানু ও হোসনে বানুকে ১-৬-৪৬ ইংরেজী তারিখে ২৩২৯ নং দানপত্র মূলে অন্যান্য জমিসহ সর্বমোট ৭২ শতক সম্পত্তি দান করার কথা বা... ভোগ দখলে নিয়ত থাকার কথা বা স্থিত থাকার কথা সম্পূর্ণ মিথ্যা কান্ধ নক উদ্দেশ্য প্রণোদিত, বানোয়াট, অব্যঞ্জকতা পূর্ণ বটে যাহা এই বিবাদীগণ সরাসরি অস্বীকার করে".

25. Order VIII, rule 5 of the CPC states that every allegation of fact in the plaint, if not denied specifically or by necessary implication, or stated to be not admitted in the pleading of the defendant, shall be taken to be admitted except as against a person under disability. The case of Zafela Begun, and others vs Atikulla and others, 16 BLC (AD) 46 = 4 XP (AD) 2 can be referred to as an example as to how evasive denial in written statement can be considered as admission of the plaintiff's case. In paragraph 7 of the plaint of the reported case the plaintiffs specifically stated that Money Execution Case Nos. 110 and 111 of 1952 were disposed of on compromise and sale of 0.07 acre in plot No. 29 towards west was confirmed and the iest 0.57 acre was set-aside, and the sale in respect of land in plot No. 27 was set-aside. The defendants simply stated in paragraph 6(Kha) of their written statement that the sale was not set-aside rather confirmed. The Apex Court held that the statements made in the written statement did not meet the positive claim of the plaintiffs on the point of setting aside the auction sale. It was further held that according to the law of pleadings, the defendant is bound to deal specifically each allegations of fact, the truth of which is not admitted. The written statement must not only deal with specifically, the defendant must also answer the point of substance. If his denial of fact is not specific but evasive, the said fact shall be taken to be admitted. In such event the admission itself being proof, no other proof is necessary. 

26. Zafela Begum was followed and applied in Divisional Estate Office); Bangladesh. Railway and others vs Jashimuddin and others, 24 BLC (AD) 36. wherein it was held that the defendants having not denied in their pleading or in their oral evidence as to the plaintiffs' chronology of devolution of title and transfer made in their favour as stated in the plaint, the same is treated as admission under Order VIII, rule 5 of the CPC. In the case in hand, the defendants, in my view, have specifically denied the foundation of the chain of title of the plaintiffs in written statement and set out their own case. Therefore, I am unable to accept Mr. Morshed's contention on point of admission of the plaintiffs' case by the defendants in their pleading. 

27. The relevant facts may be recalled. The plaintiffs' case is that Abdul Kader gifted 22.5 decimals of land to his two daughters on 1-6-1946 (Exhibit. 3). The defendant's case is that Abdul Kader did not make such gift. He sold 153/4 decimals of land out of the said 22.5 decimals to Ayesha Khatun by a registered sale deed dated 3-5-1960 (Exhibit. Kha). The defendants tendered the original. sale deed dated 3-5-1960 in evidence. 
The trial Court did not disbelieve the defendants' chain of title based on Exhibit-Kha. The Court observed that earlier transfer of the suit land made in 1946 (Exhibit. 3) in favour of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs would prevail over the subsequent transfers made to the predecessor-in-interest of the defendants. The observation is based on the maxim "qui prior est tempore potior est" jure meaning "he who prior in time is better in law" incorporated in section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. I have already held that the certified copy of the gift deed dated 1-4-1946 (Exhibit. 3) tendered in evidence by the plaintiffs is not admissible. Therefore, the very foundation of the plaintiffs' case is 'not proved'. The argument of Mr. Morshed to consider the probative value of Exhibit-3 is rejected for the reason that the same is inadmissible evidence. Question of examining the probative value arises when a document is/or may be admissible which is not the scenario in the instant case. Since the plaintiffs' case is not proved, I refrain from dwelling upon the question of possession and limitation argued by Mr. Omar Farook appearing for the defendants. 

28. The defendants have successfully made out a case that Exhibit Nos. 3, 5 and 7 tendered in evidence by the plaintiffs are inadmissible. Both the Courts below committed error of law resulting in an error in decreeing the suit causing failure of justice in treating the gift deed dated 1-4-1946 (Exhibit 3) and subsequent sale deeds dated 27-4-1974 and 7-5-1987 respectively (Exhibit. 5 and 7) as admissible evidence which form a chain of title of the plaintiffs. Hence the Rule succeeds. 

29. In the Result the Rule is made absolute. The judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below are set-aside. The suit is dismissed. 

Send down the LCR. 

End.
