full_judgment:
Md. Bazlur Rahman, J: At the instance of the petitioners, a Rule Nisi was issued in this writ in the following terms:—
"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order No.24 dated 22-1-2024 passed by the learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka in Artha Rin Suit No.183 of 2022 rejecting the application for striking out the names of the defendants No. 2 to 8 and 16 to 20 from the defendants class of the plaint (Annexure-F to the writ petition, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and why the respondent No.2 should not be directed to strike out the names of defendant petitioners from the plaint of the Artha Rin Suit No.183 of 2022 and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper." 

2. Besides the issuance of the Rule, all further proceedings of the said Artha Rin Suit so far as it relates only to the petitioners were stayed for a period of three months which had been enlarged later on from time to time. 

3. Admitted facts 
Plaintiff respondent No. 3, Dutch Bangla Bank Ltd, Matuail Branch, Jatrabari, Dhaka is the lender institution and Fareast Finance and Investment Ltd. is the borrower company availing of 100 million term credit facility vide sanction letter dated 25-10-2016, Anx H-5. Defendant No. 13 of the Suit, Santanu Saha (pro-forma respondent No. 10) and defendant No.14, Mohammad Hafizour Rahman (pro-forma respondent No. 11) were the then Managing Director and Deputy Managing Director of the lender institution respectively who dealt with the credit transaction executing loan agreement and different charge documents necessary for security of the loan. On 17-12-2020, the lender-Bank served a legal notice upon these defendant petitioners and others to which instant defendant-petitioner No.2, Mohammad Ali Zaryab (present Managing Director of the borrower company), responded and admitting the loan deposited Taka 143,36,405 to liquidate the liability in part. He on 29-12-2020 applied to the lender bank for second rescheduling Annex H-7, of the loan and its first rescheduling was approved on 19-2-2019, Annex H-6, at the instance of the erstwhile Managing Director, Santanu Saha. The bank though agreed to the rescheduling proposal but defendants did not provide all required legal documents to assist the bank. Thereafter, the bank further served legal notice to these defendant-petitioners and others but to no effect. Finally, the bank in order to recover the outstanding liabilities of Taka 6,15, 52, 614. 61 as on 10-5-2022 instituted the above Artha Rin suit No.183 of 2022 against the instant 7 defendant-petitioners and 14 others wherein these defendant-petitioners and defendant nos. 16-20 of the suit submitted an application to strike out their names from defendants' category under Order I, rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil procedure read with section 6(5) and 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. The leaned trial court upon hearing the parties rejected the application vide impugned order No. 24 dated 22-1-2024, Annexure F. 

4. Defendant-Petitioners' case (defendant Nos.2-8 of the Artha Rin Suit) 
4.1 The borrower appointed Muhammad Ali Zaryab, defendant petitioner No.2, as the Managing Director of the company vide appointment letter dated 16-8-2020, Annexure H, for a period of 3 years. He joined on 31-8-2020 and thereafter his tenure was further extended upon Bangladesh Bank's approval till 31-8-2024, Annexure H-4. Defendant-petitioners 1 and 3-7 were nominated as independent directors of the borrower company on 29-3-2021, Annexure G-2 by respondent No. 5, Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC). The Board of Directors of the company was constituted by BSEC designating defendant petitioner No. 1, Md. Ashraful Moqbul, as the Charmin of the Board of Directors with special mention that all these defendant-petitioner Nos. 1 and 3-7 will not be included in the particulars of directors, FORM-XII, and also will have no personal financial liability. Moreover, defendant Nos. 15- 21 of the said suit were also independent directors fixing the tenure of defendant No. 16 from 17-1-2019 to 12-3-2021, defendant No. 17 from 5-9-2019 to 2-3-2021, defendant No.18 from 17-1-2019 to 12-3-2021, defendant No. 19 from 4-2-2019 to 28-3-2021, defendant No. 20 from 22-7-2019 to 28-3-2021 and defendant no 21 from 2-3-2019 to 28-3-2021who were neither the borrower, nor 3rd party mortgagor nor 3rd party guarantor nor were involved with the loan when it was sanctioned on 25-10-2016. These petitioners along with several others of the parity class submitted an application before the trial court on 5-11-2023 Annexure D, for striking out their names from the category of defendants which the court illegally rejected by the impugned order dated 22-1-2024, Annexure F. This very order has been assailed in the writ jurisdiction before us. 

5. Case of respondent No.3 (the lender bank) 
5.1 This respondent has opposed the Rule by submitting an affidavit-in-opposition denying material allegations brought against it and contending, Infer alia, that the former directors of the borrower company applied for loan facilities and thereupon the lender bank sanctioned the same which they availed and enjoyed on behalf of the company. These petitioners and other similar defendants of the suit have ample opportunities to rebut their liabilities upon adducing evidence in trial court. The writ is, therefore, not maintainable upon factual matter. The involvement in and enjoyment of the credit facilities of the defendants of the Artha Rin Suit inclusive of the instant petitioners are only determinable by trial court upon appreciation of evidence being adduced by the parties. Hence, the impugned order passed by trial court in Artha Rin Suit No. 183 of 2022 suffers no legal infirmities and shall succeed in the long run. 

6. Submissions 
6.1 Mr. Lutfor Rahman, leaned counsel appearing for the petitioners, referring mainly to section 6(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, candidly submitted that the learned trial court while recording the impugned order of rejection dated 22-1-2024 Annexure F, in Artha Rin suit No. 183 of 2022 has violated the statutory provision that no one without the third party mortgagor or the third party guarantor can be impleaded as defendant in an Antha Rin Suit filed by the lender institution against the principal debtor. 
6.2 He further clarified that when those third parties are related with the loan, then only they are required to be made parties as such. 
6.3 It was further asserted that neither of the instant petitioners, either in the capacity of mortgagor or in the capacity of guarantor, was involved with the grant of loan in any manner whatsoever. 
6.4 Mr. Rahman further contended that defendant No. 13, Santanu Saha and defendant No. 14 Mohammad Hafizour Rahman, the erstwhile Managing Director and Deputy Managing Director of the borrower company respectively, played role as such in applying for the loan and getting it sanctioned on 25-10-2016. Defendant-petitioner No. 2, Mohammad Ali Zaryab, the current Managing Director of the borrower company, though was not holding such position during loan period but joining after a long time on 31-8-2020 did some ex officio functions including partial repayment of loan, its rescheduling etc. which were accepted by lender institution with some conditions being illegally imposed upon him. 
6.5 Mr. Lutfor Rahman underscored that no person other than the three categories expressly enumerated in section 6(5) of the said Ain, 2003 are required to be impleaded as defendant in an Artha Rin Suit and any order, if passed, in defiance thereof will be a nullity. 
6.6 Mr. Rahman, however, cited a catena of decisions reported in 120201 19 ALR (AD) 76, 5 CLR 26-29 and 4 ALR 2014(2). 
6.7 Per contra, learned Counsel Mr. Monjur Elahi Porag, referring to the decisions reported in 16 BLC (AD) 4, and 21 BLC (AD) (2016) 210-211, argued on behalf of the lender institution, respondent No. 3, that the former directors were related to the applying for and availing of the loan which have been manifestly incorporated in the averments of plaint of the Artha Rin Suit with an affidavit being appended therewith under section 6(2) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain. Whether those former directors were or were not related as such to the loan in question is now a question of fact to be determined by trial count upon requisite evidence being adduced by both the parties for and against the issues in the suit and thus an alternative avenue of rebuttal is widely open to the those directors-defendants to disprove their alleged liabilities. Mr. Monjur Elahi urged that the matter is thus not amenable to writ jurisdiction. 
6.8 He further emphasized that any party, necessary or proper, both can be impleaded as defendant in any civil suit obviously including an Artha Rin suit and section 6(5) of the Ain, 2003 puts no irresistible embargo from impleading any one as defendant in an Artha Rin suit other than those 3 people categorically mentioned therein. 
6.9 Before parting with, Mr. Elahi summed up that the trial count rightly perceived the scheme of the statute and correctly passed the impugned order in order to prevent the probable failure to recover the public money. 

7. Deliberations and Decision 
7.1. We have extensively gone through the pleadings of the parties, examined the documents annexed therewith and considered their core point of disputes. 
7.2 It, therefore, transpires that the thrust debate in the instant case lies in fixing loan liability of person impleaded as defendant in an Artha Rin Suit who have no direct involvement with the credit transaction either as a borrower, or as a third party mortgagor, or as a third party guarantor. Petitioners have thus resisted that none but those 3 categories are necessary party in an Artha Rin Suit as per section 6(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. In this regard, the simple single argument on behalf of lender respondent No. 3 is that since company's former Managing Director, Shantanu Shaha (Defendant 13), and former Deputy Managing Director, Mohammad Hafizur Rahman (Defendant 14) executed all necessary charge documents and since the pro-forma defendant No.6 (the company), Md. Ashraful Makbul (defendant-petitioner 1), Mohammad Ali Zaryab (defendant-petitioner 2) being respectively the borrower, company's current Chairman and Managing Director; Ihsanul Aziz (defendant-petitioner 3), Sheikh Nazmul Hoque Saikat (defendant-petitioner 4), Md. Sajib Hossain CFA (defendant-petitioner 5), Dr. Md. Mosharrof Hossain (defendant-petitioner 6), AKM Shahiduzzaman MBA (IBA) (defendant-petitioner 7) being the current Directors of the company and finally defendant nos. 15-20 being the former Directors thereof are all jointly and severally liable to make payment of the entire outstanding liabilities along with up-to-date interest accrued thereon. 
7.3 However, the party addition criteria as mandated in sub-section (5) of section 6 of the Ain, 2003 is directly relevant to the basic submission of the petitioners. Sub-section (5) is contextually reproduced as under: — 
"(৫) আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান মূল ঋণগ্রহীতার (Principal debtor) বিরুদ্ধে মামলা দায়ের করার সময়, তৃতীয় পক্ষ বন্ধকদাতা (Third partz mortgagor) বা তৃতীয় পক্ষ গ্যারান্টর (Third partz guarantor) ঋণের সহিত সংশ্লিষ্ট থাকিলে, উহাদিগকে বিবাদী পক্ষ করিবে; এবং আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত রায়, আদেশ বা ডিক্রী সকল বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে যৌথভাবে ও পৃথক পৃথক ভাবে (Jointly and severally) কার্যকর হইবে এবং ডিক্রী জারীর মামলা সকল বিবাদী-দায়কের বিরুদ্ধে একইসাথে পরিচালিত হইবে:
তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, ডিক্রী জারীর মাধ্যমে দাবী আদায় হওয়ার ক্ষেত্রে আদালত প্রথমে মূল ঋণগ্রহীতা-বিবাদীর এবং অতঃপর যথাক্রমে তৃতীয় পক্ষ বন্ধকদাতা (Third party mortgagor) ও তৃতীয় পক্ষ গ্যারান্টর (Third Party guarantor) এর সম্পত্তি যতদূর সম্ভব আকৃষ্ট করিবে:
আরো শর্ত থাকে যে, বাদীর অনুকূলে প্রদত্ত ডিক্রীর দাবী তৃতীয় পক্ষ বন্ধকদাতা (Third party mortgagor) অথবা তৃতীয় পক্ষ গ্যারান্টর (Third party guarantor) পরিশোধ করিয়া থাকিলে উক্ত ডিক্রী যথাক্রমে তাহাদের অনুকূলে স্থানান্তরিত হইবে এবং তাহারা মূল ঋণগ্রহীতার (Principal debtor) বিরুদ্ধে উহা প্রয়োগ বা জারী করিতে পারিবেন।"
7.4 Conversely, Mr. Elahi, the learned counsel for the respondent contended that sub-section (5) of section 6 of the Ain, 2003 provides no preventive list of the party addition criteria, rather it gives a flexible guideline amenable to relax to or include any person as defendant in an Artha Rin Suit essential for the purpose of recovering the legitimate overdues of any public lending entity. As referred to by him, we find in the case of Bokul Aktar vs Bangladesh and other (16 BLC (AD) 5) that petitioner Bokul Aktar, the Chairman of M/s Oyester Fashion Ltd, submitted an application before concerned Artha Rin Adalat Chittagong praying for striking out of her name as a defendant which had been rejected by court. Being aggrieved, the petitioner moved the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction but failed. In Civil petition for Leave to Appeal (No. 245 of 2009), Hon'ble Appellate Division held the petitioner to be added as a necessary defendant in the Artha Rin Suit "because the company enjoyed the loan when she was its Chairman, as such, the suit should be disposed of in her presence. However, her liability is not dependent on her status as the chairman or shareholder of the company unless it is found on evidence that she executed the charge documents in favour of the bank or mortgaged her property in its favour in order to ensure repayment of the loan. Only in that case she will be liable". In our case, the instant borrower appears to have started enjoying the sanctioned loan when defendant Nos. 13 and 14, Santanu Shaha and Mohammad Hafizour Rahman, were the Managing Director and Deputy Managing Director of the company and defendant nos. 15-21 (Md. Ershad Ullah, Syed Imam Hossain, Md. Rafiqul Islam, Khandoker Motaher Uddin Ahmed, Mohammad Muhibbullahil Baqi and Farzul Ekram) were the directors thereof. It is worth mentioning that the veil of corporate entity is subject to piercing by court and any negligence made or fraud committed by directors may be put into light for any legal action to prevent repetition of commission of such fraud or negligence. In the case of One Bank Ltd vs Chaya Developer (Pvt) Ltd and other (21 BLC (AD) 2016, P-211) it was held that section 6(5) of the Ain provides guidelines as to how the defendants can be impleaded in the proceedings of an Artha Rin Suit. Mr. Elahi thus insisted on his argument that in appropriate cases such guidelines require to be interpreted elastically to achieve generous goal and the interpretation should not be confined to any rigorous viewpoint. 

7.5 Conversely, the petitioners' learned counsel Mr. Rahman drew our attention to the decision held in the case of Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd. vs Md Sirazul Islam (2020) 19 ALR (AD) 76-77) and also to the decision reported in 5 CLR (AD) 2017 P-29 that no Artha Rin Suit can be filed against any person who is neither a loanee nor a guarantor. But upon plain reading of the facts of both the cases, we find our facts to be in direct consonance with those of Bokul Akter's case and, accordingly, the contention of the leaned counsel for the contesting respondent merits substance that the instant Artha Rin Suit No. 183 of 2022 should be disposed of in presence of those defendants Nos. 13-14 and 15-21 though their liabilities are determinable only on proof of evidence during trial. It is equally pertinent to add here that the tenure of those former directors and their status as independent directors are purely a disputed question of fact not amenable to adjudication under writ jurisdiction. 

7.6. Admittedly, the barrower is a Z category company listed with Stock Exchange and for upgradation therefrom the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission has reconstituted company's Board of Directors (BoD), Annexure G-2 dated 29-3-2021 and thereby nominating/appointing defendant-petitioner-1, Ashraful Mokbul, defendant-petitioner-3, Ihsanul Aziz, defendant-petitioner-4 Sheikh Nazmul Hoque Saikat, defendant-petitioner-5 Md Sajib Hossan CFA, defendant -petitioner-6, Dr. Mosharrof Hossain and defendant-petitioner-7 AKM Shahid-uz-zaman as the independent directors. Regarding pecuniary liability, clause (e) of the BoD reconstitution letter dated 29-3-2021, Annexure G-2, speaks as under: —
"(e) As per the Commission's directives No. SEC/CMRRCD/2009-193/11 dated 22 March, 2021, the name of independent directors appointed/nominated by the Commission under the referred Notification shall not be included in the particulars of directors (FORM-XII) and will not have any personal financial liability." 

7.7 Clause (b) of the said BoD reconstitution memo dated 29-3-2021 Annexure G-2, also demonstrates that Md. Ashraful Mokbul (defendant petitioner-1, the former Chairman of the Board of Directors, Sonali Bank Limited) was proposed to be selected as the Chairman of the BoD of the instant borrower company. It goes without saying that independent directors are non-executive directors on a company's board having no share with the company they are appointed in and are not lined up with any of the executive directors. They do not have any financial relationship either with the company, its promoters or its management. The key role they play is to provide impartial judgment, ensure corporate governance and to work to protect and safeguard the interest of the investors especially small investors. In view of the above nature and character of appointment of defendant-petitioner Nos. 1, 3-7, vide conditions under Annexure G-2, their names are liable to be struck out from the category of defendant in the Artha Rin Suit No. 183 of 2020. On the other hand, the contract of appointment and reappointment of defendant petitioner 2, Mohammad Ali Zaryab as the Managing Director of the company, Annexure H-1-H-4, do not reflect any condition absolving him from any financial liability likely to fall upon him by way of succession since he as the CEO of the company is routinely responsible to run and manage the business and. affairs of the company. Even the Board of Directors of the debtor-company while making proposal for his (defendant-petitioner No.2) such appointment as Managing Director inserted therein no special privilege of exoneration from financial liability, if any. Hence, defendant petitioner 2 cannot claim himself to be in parity with the defendant petitioner Nos. 1 and 3-7 enjoying special prerogative by virtue of their terms of appointment/nomination, Annexure G-2. 

7.8 Thus in view of the preceding facts and features of the instant circumstances and upon analysis of the relevant provisions of law in this regard, the simple takeaway is that the learned Artha Rin Adalat (respondent No.2) failing to conceive the correct legal position erroneously recorded the impugned order dated 22-1-2024 in Artha Rin Suit No.183 of 2022, as evidenced by Annexure F, rejecting, as a whole, the application dated 5-11-2023, as evidenced by Annexure-D, seeking striking out from the category of defendant the names of these defendant petitioners and defendant nos.16-20 in the said Artha Rin Suit. The omission by the trial court to strike out the names of defendant-petitioner Nos. 1 and 3-7 from the defendant category in the said suit is, therefore, liable to be declared without lawful authority and of no legal effect. The Rule thus deserves to be made absolute in part. 

8. Order of this Court 
8.1. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute in part without, however, any order as to costs 
8.2 The learned Artha Rin Adalat, 1st court, Dhaka is hereby directed to strike out the names of defendant-petitioner nos. 1 and 3-7 from the category of defendant in Artha Rin Suit No 183 of 2022 and to proceed the suit in accordance with law. 
8.3 Let a copy of this judgment and order be communicated to the learned trial court immediately. 

End.

parties:
Ashraf Ali Pramanik (Md) and others ------ Defendants-Appellants-Petitioners
VS
Hazera Bewa and Others ...Plaintiffs-Respondents Proforma-Opposite ------ Parties
full_judgment:
Md Bazlur Rahman, J: This civil revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure has been directed at the instance of the defendants-appellants-petitioners wherein a Rule was issued calling upon opposite party Nos.1-10 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 14-8-2008 passed by learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra in Partition Appeal No.92 of 2006 affirming those dated 11-7-2006 passed by learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Bogra in Partition Suit No.92 of 1993 should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Besides issuance of the Rule, all further proceedings of Partition Suit No.92 of 1993 pending before the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Bogra was stayed. 

3. Facts of the revision application:  
3.1 Plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties instituted Title Suit No. 92 of 1993 for partition of land to the extent of 4.25 acres which was decreed on 11-7-2006 on being aggrieved of which these defendants-appellants-petitioners preferred an appeal bearing No.92 of 2006 to the learned District Judge, Bogra which, upon transfer, was heard and disposed of by Learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra disallowing the appeal on 14-8-2008 and thereby affirming the judgment and decree passed by learned trial court. This very order passed by learned Appellate Court has been challenged in the instant civil revision. 
3.2 Short facts leading to the plaint of Partition Suit No.92 of 1993 are that the lands, elaborately mentioned in the schedule to the plaint, measuring an area of 9.94 acres originally belonged to Hobullah Pramanik who, while in due possession thereof, died leaving behind 2 wives, Patani Bibi and Sharbi Bibi; 4 sons, Syed Ullah, Mohit Ullah, Shaheb Ullah and Nayeb Ullah and 2 daughters, Fayzal/Kayjan and Mayzal. Patani Bibi died leaving behind 2 sons and 2 daughters, namely Shaheb Ullah and Nayeb Ullah and Fayzal and Mayzal. On the other hand, Sharbi Bibi died leaving behind 2 sons, namely Syed Ullah and Mohit Ullah among whom Mohit Ullah died celibate leaving only brother Syed Ullah. Mayzal died leaving behind her husband, Sader Prang and one son, Md. Nasir Uddin (Defendant No.1). Shaheb Ullah died leaving behind his brother Nayeb Ullah. Fayzal/Kayjan died leaving behind 2 sons, Karim Pramanik (Defendant No.2) and Oli Pramanik and one daughter, Mst. Kasoron Bewa(Defendant No.3). Oli Pramanik died leaving behind one daughter, Mst. Zobeda Bibi (Defendant No.4), one brother, Karirn Pramanik (Defendant No.2) and one sister, Mst. Kasoron Bewa (Defendant No.3). Syed Ullah died leaving behind 3 sons, namely Md. Korban Ali Pramanik (Plaintiff No.2), Md. Ismail Hossain Pramanik (Plaintiff No.3) and Mohir Uddin Pramanik (Plaintiff No.1) who filed the partition suit. During pendency of the suit, plaintiff Mohir Uddin died leaving behind his wife, Most. Hazera Bewa, 3 sons, Md. Hazrat Ali, Md. Mohabbat Ali and Md. Akbar Ali and 4 daughters, Benu Khatun, Nurjahan Khatun, Sokhela Banu and Mst. Rahima Khatun. Sader Prang and defendant No.1, Md. Nasir Uddin transferred 31 decimals of land from CS plot No.3825 (though erroneously written in the documents as plot No.3824) to Syed Ullah and Nayeb Ullah by virtue of an instrument of sale dated 2-4-1946. In view of the above genealogy and vide the above registered kabala, the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties claiming 4.25 acres of land in the scheduled partiable holdings instituted the above partition suit. 
3.3 Among others, these petitioners as defendants Nos.5-7 and 12-17 entered appearance and contested the suit by way of submitting a joint written statement denying materials allegations made in the plaint and contended therein, inter-alia, that the suit is not maintainable with the simple prayer for partition and that the suit suffers from defect of parties and hotchpot. It is further contended that long before the suit the disputed properties were partitioned amicably by mets and bounds between the predecessors of the parties by a deed of partition dated 30-6-1939. Shaheb Ullah Pramanik, Mohit Ullah Pramanik and Mohorbi Bewa transferred two- wan (a local land measurement in Bogra) of land out of the suit land in favour of Shahebullah Pramanik, the predecessor of these defendants-appellants-petitioners vide registered sale deed dated 10-2-1925. The said land of two wans measuring 58 decimals were recorded in plot No. 3124 and 4735 in CS Khatian No.889 but CS Khatian No.1477 was erroneously written in the said sale deed out of bonafide mistake. After the said sale deed was registered, Syeedullah Pramanik, Mohitullah Pramanik and Shaharbi Bewa got their title extinguished to the said amount of land. It is further stated that Syed Ali Pramanik, the predecessor of the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties, was the party to the said partition deed dated 30-6-1939 and in view of thereof MRR Khatian was prepared in the name of the parties to the partition deed. As per partition deed, Syed Ali Pramanik acquired 1.28 acres of land in CS Khatian No.1388 (schedule 2 to the plaint) and 1.06 acres of land in CS Khatian No.218 (schedule No.1) totaling 2.34 acres of land and MRR Khatian Nos. 237 and 442 were correctly prepared in his name. After the demise of Syed Ali Pramanik, the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties inherited 2.34 acres of land in the partible holdings and that they have no right, title and interest in any land in CS khatian no 889 (Schedule 3). They are only entitled to 2.34 acres of land. In the above circumstances, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 
3.4 During trial, these defendants-appellants-petitioners and the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties examined 2 witnesses each and produced several documents in their respective favour which on behalf of plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties were marked as exhibit-1 series, 2 and I and exhibit- Ka, Kha, G series, Gha series, Uma and Cha series on behalf of these defendants-appellants-petitioners. 
3.5 The learned trial court vide its judgment dated 11-7-2006 decreed the suit in preliminary form allotting 4.25 acres of land in favour of the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties. The learned Court also allotted shaham in favour of defendant No.1, 2(ka), 2(uma) thereof who preferred no appeal against the saham allotted to them. On being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by learned trial court, these petitioners preferred an appeal bearing No.92 of 2006 which as stated before was dismissed affirming the judgment and decree of the learned trial court. Thereafter, these defend-ants-appellants-petitioners have approached this court in the instant civil revision and obtained the aforesaid Rule and Stay. 

4. Submissions  
4.1 Mr. Md. Zahidul Bari, the learned Counsel appearing for the defendants-appellants-petitioners, submits that the learned Court of appeal below as well as the learned trial court failed to appreciate the deed of partition dated 30-6-1939, exhibit-Kha, into consideration as the basis of evidence in its appropriate perspective. 
4.2 The learned Counsel adds that the deed was acted upon and the outcome thereof has been subsequently reflected in the preparation and publication of the MRR Khatians prepared in view of the said deed. 
4.3 Mr. NV. Zahidul Bari also urges that Syed Ullah Pramanik and others, the predecessors of the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties, transferred 58 decimals of land vide registered kabala dated 10-2-1925, exhibit-Uma, to Shaheb Ullah Pramanik, the predecessor of these 'petitioners and accordingly MRR khatian No.1478 has been prepared in the name of these petitioners in respect of the said land but this transfer has been erroneously kept out of consideration. 
4.4 He further submits that those 58 decimals of land conveyed vide deed dated 10-2-1925 were relayed by Advocate Commissioner and found by him to be identical to form part of the suit land. 
4.5 The learned. Counsel underscores that those deeds of sale and partition stated above were of 30 years old documents and have been submitted from proper custody, but discarding those documents by both courts below from evidential consideration is a manifest fallacy of law which has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 
4.6 Mr. Md. Zahidul Bari further adds that the suit was not maintainable seeking partition simpliciter inasmuch as the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties' claim both CS and SA khantians to be erroneous. 
4.7 He also submits that the document dated 2-4-1946 despite containing mistaken plot number was considered for the plaintiffs to give them benefit, whereas the deed of sale dated 10-2-1925 containing mistaken khatian number was not considered in favour of these defendants-appellants-petitioners. Therefore, these petitioners have been discriminated for disregarding the Rule of Parity. 
4.8 The learned Counsel, however, wraps up his submission that the Court of appeal being the final court of facts failed to properly discuss and independently assess the evidence and hence, the impugned judgment and decree passed by learned appellate court is liable to be interfered with and be set-aside accordingly. 
4.9 Per contra, Mr. Md. Abdul Momin, appearing on behalf of the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties, submits that a partition suit is well maintainable without seeking declaration of title being added therewith. 
4.9.1 He also submits that there is no perversity in the findings of the appellate court or any kind of non-consideration or misreading of material evidence has happened in taking these findings. And so, the concurrent findings of facts by both the courts below are immune from any interference by this court. 
4.9.2 Mr. Md. Abdul Momin, however, refers to a catena of decisions reported in 62 DLR (AD) (2010) p-245, 23 BLD (AD) 2003, p-83-87 and 12 LM (AD) 2022(1). 

5. Deliberations and Decision  
5.1 In view of the foregoing rival submissions of the learned Counsels, the first and foremost contention to be resolved in this revision is whether Partition Suit No.92 of 1993 is at all maintainable in the instant form and manner with lone relief of partition, or any additional prayer for declaration of title was required to be sought besides partition. The pleadings of the parties are found to be akin to the submissions of the learned Counsel for the defendants-appellants-petitioners that the CS and SA Khatian did not properly record, the names of the predecessors of the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties. Here the learned Counsel assails the maintainability of the suit on the ground of seeking therein the solitary prayer for partition. In the case of Chinnzoy Chowdhury and others vs Sree Mridul Chowdhury and others [23 BLD (AD) 2003, page-83-87 : 55 DLR (AD) 115], both trial court and the High Court Division held the suit to be maintainable with simple prayer for partition. Some ancestral properties were the subject matter of partition in the suit. But in the appeal before the Hon'ble Appellate Division the question of maintainability had been assailed wherein His Lordship observed as follows—
"In a suit for partition all the incidental questions of title, however complicated it may be, can be decided and finally disposed of. The parties should not be thrown away or driven out on the ground of maintainability of the suit and, as such, the argument as to non-maintainability of the suit as advanced by Mr. Khan perishes without footing." 
5.2 In our instant case, the entire scenario regarding accrual of the title of plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties to suit land has been narrated in the plaint in broad details. No hurdle seems to be apparent to determine the acquisition of title by plaintiff and hence their names, whether recorded or omitted to be recorded in a particular khatian is quite immaterial, particularly when the laid down principle is that Record-of Rights does not create or extinguish any title to the lands incorporated therein. Be it mentioned, CS Khatian though being a key land record document holding significant evidential value is not conclusive proof of ownership. Thus the contention agitated on the issue of maintainability merits no substance. 
5.3 Pleadings of the parties and the evidences led thereon show the names and numbers of praeposituses, the devolution of properties upon their deaths on their lineage and the calculation of shares according to inheritance are not disputed at all. But there are three documents, namely a sale deed dated 3-4-1946, an unregistered amicable partition deed dated 30-6-1939 and another sale deed dated 10-2-1925, all being exhibited in original during trial as Ka, Kha, and Umo respectively, which generate a new kind of controversy between the contending parties. These documents are supposed to be the catalyst which fluctuates the share of the co-sharers in the partible holdings. The trial court upon analysis of evidences, oral or documentary, adduced by the parties, determined specific decision upon each of the documents and found plaint case to preponderate over that of these petitioners in respect of those documents. In the appeal, the learned appellate court made reappraisal of the evidences over all the issues formulated by learned trial court and concurred therewith. The courts below concurrently found that Sayed ullah, the predecessor of the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties, acquired 4.10 acres of land by inheritance and 0.15½ acre by purchase totaling 4.25 acres in the holdings under partition and they as co-sharer have been in possession thereof. It appears from the record that the learned court of appeal as the last court of fact decided the question of fact and recorded its finding on evaluation of evidence on record. The findings of appellate court, in the absence of any perversity, are not liable to be disturbed in revision. Here the citation of the decisions, as referred to by the learned Counsel for the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties, held in the case of Abdul Gafur and others vs Abdur Razzak and others [62 DLR (AD) 2451 and in the case of Md. Amzad Ali Sheikh and others vs Koyron Bewa and others (12 LM (AD) 2022(1), page-173 apply to our instant case. 
5.4 In view of the preceding facts and features of the instant circumstances and upon examination of our apex court's observation applicable to this field, I find no merit in the contention of the learned Counsel for the defendants-appellants-petitioners. Hence, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

6. Court's Order 
6.1 In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. 
6.2 The judgment bf affirmance' passed by learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Bogura in Appeal No. 92 of 2006 is hereby upheld. 
6.3 The order of Stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated. 
6.4 Let a copy of this judgment and order be transmitted immediately to the learned lower courts. 
6.5 Also send down the lower court record at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
KM Rasheduzzaman Raja, J: In this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure Rule was issued on 11-12-2005 upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why order No. 23 dated 13-8-2005 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Noakhali setting aside the compromise decree dated 19-2-2005 in Title Suit No. 47 of 2003 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. At the time of issuance of the Rule, operation of the impugned order passed in Title Suit No. 47 of 2003 was stayed initially for 6(six) months which was subsequently extended from time to time. 

3. The facts relevant for disposal of the Rule, in brief, are that the plaintiff petitioner Abdul Ali, now deceased, filed Title Suit No. 47 of 2003 praying for declaration of his title to the land mentioned in the schedule of the plaint. The defendant Opposite Parties appeared in the suit and submitted a joint written statement therein. Subsequently, the plaintiff and the defendants settled their dispute on compromise through mediation as per the provisions of section 89A of the Code of Civil Procedure. Accordingly, they jointly filed an application of compromise before the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Noakhali on 19-2-2005. The learned Joint District Judge accepted the compromise application and decreed the suit in terms of compromise vide order No. 15 dated 19-2-2005. Subsequently, the defendants filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting aside the said compromise decree on the ground of committing fraud. The learned Joint District Judge allowed the application filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and reinstated Title Suit No. 431 of 2003 in it's earlier number and file by order No. 23 dated 13-8-2005 upon setting aside the compromise decree. 

4. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid order the plaintiff petitioner has filed this Civil Revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule and the interim order of stay. 

5. Defendant Opposite Party No. 3 contested the Rule by filing a counter affidavit denying the material allegations averred in Civil Revision contending, inter-alia, that the plaintiff petitioner filed Title Suit No. 47 of 2003 against some dead defendants and some fictitious persons. The plaintiff filed an application on the date of filing on the suit for exemption of service of summons upon the defendants. The plaintiff managed to get a false and fabricated written statement filed and thereafter also managed to procure a decree in the suit in the name of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) even forging the signatures of the defendants in the Wakalotnama. Upon found such fraudulent practice by the plaintiff in procuring the compromise decree, the learned Joint District Judge set-aside the decree passed in Title Suit No. 47 of 2003 upon allowing the application filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the impugned order dated 19-2-2005. As, such the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

6. Learned Advocate Mr. Mohammad Abdul Baset appearing on behalf of the plaintiff petitioner assailed the propriety of the impugned order submits that the learned Joint District Judge passed the compromise decree in Title Suit No. 47 of 2003 following the mediation process enshrined in section 89A of the Code of Civil Procedure by order dated 19-2-2005. There are specific provisions, such as, filing of appeal on the ground of illegality against the compromise or consent decree as passed in this case. Even, the defendant Opposite Parties could file a separate suit for cancellation of the decree in question. In no way, the learned Joint District Judge can set aside the compromise decree by invoking inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Mohammad Abdul Baset relied on the decision of the case of Md. Shahidur Rahman Majurnder alias Md. Shahidullah Majurnder and others vs Sabirunnesa and others, 16 BLD (AD) 50 : 1 BLC (AD) 43 in support of his submissions. 

7. On the other hand, learned Advocate Mr. Abul Kalam Chowdhury appearing for Opposite Party No.-3 confronted the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner submitting that the learned Joint District Judge did not follow the mediation process properly. No summons was served upon defendant No.-3 in Title Suit No. 47 of 2003. The plaintiff arranged the so called mediation illegally and furnished the compromise petition behind their back and knowledge. Since, there is ex facie fraud on record in procuring the compromise decree by the order dated 19-2-2005 passed in Title Suit No. 47 of 2003, learned Joint District Judge committed no error in allowing the application filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thereby reinstating the suit. Learned Advocate Mr. Abul Kalam Chowdhury referred to the cases of Master Abdul Aziz vs Abanin Mohan Mukherjee, 30 DLR (SC) 221, Government of Bangladesh and another vs MA Khair Bhuiyan, 55 DLR (AD) 76, and Deputy Commissioner Brahmanbaria vs Chand Mia and others, 30 BLC (AD) 138. 

8. Learned Advocate Mr. Gazi Md. Mohsin appearing on behalf of Opposite Party Nos. 4(a)-4(f) adopted the submissions of the learned Advocate Mr. Abul Kalam Chowdhury adding that the plaintiff collusively procured the decree in question getting the land of these Opposite Parties included therein although they were not made parties to the suit. Moreover, after reinstating Title Suit No. 47 of 2003 in it's earlier number and file, the plaintiff petitioner can establish his case on merit and thus he has no cause of grievance against the impugned order. 

9. We have heard the learned Advocates of both sides and perused the Civil Revision and counter affidavit along with the documents annexed thereto. 

10. It appears from the order sheet of Title Suit No. 47 of 2003 (Annexure-2) that the suit was filed on 16-10-2003. On the date of filing the plaintiff petitioner filed an application for exemption of both modes of usual and postal service of summons upon the defendants which was fixed for hearing on 4-11-2003. Thereafter, though the plaintiff absent, the Court sou motu adjourned the hearing for 13 consecutive occasions. On 12- 2-2005 the defendants all on a sudden appeared and submitted a written statement with Wakalotnama. Upon receiving the written statement the then learned Joint District Judge fixed the suit for ADR proceeding under section 89A of the Code of Civil Procedure on 26- 2-2005. On 16-2-2005 the plaintiff and defendants filed a joint application praying for appointing Mr. Hossain Ahmed as their mediator to hold the Alternative Dispute Resolution procedure. Learned Joint District Judge allowed the petition and issued writ of appointment. On 19-2-2005 the plaintiff and defendants filed another joint application praying for advancing the date for disposal of the suit by adopting the Alternative Dispute Resolution process. Accordingly, the then learned Joint District Judge allowed the application. On the same date, the purported parties to the suit also filed a deed of compromise with their signatures along with signatures of their respective lawyers. Learned Joint District Judge also accepted the deed of compromise and decreed the suit in terms of compromise on that very date. 

11. Defendant No. 3 Md. Hanif alongwith other 3rd parties appeared and filed a joint application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the subsequent learned Joint District Judge on 3-5-2005 praying for reinstating. Title Suit No. 47 of 2003 in it's earlier file and number after upon setting aside the compromise decree passed therein and adding the 3rd parties to the suit as defendants on the grounds of fraud and forgery. Defendant Nos. 15/16/18 have also filed another application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 15-6-2005 for setting aside the aforesaid compromise decree and allowing them to contest the suit by filing written statements on the same grounds. 

12. Learned Joint District Judge heard both the applications filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and upon found forgery in the alleged signatures of defendant No.-3 in the written statement in comparison with each others, non-service of process upon other defendants and inclusion of the 3rd parties property without impleading them as defendants therein passed the impugned order holding that the plaintiffs got the compromise decree by practising fraud upon the Court and thereby set-aside the decree. 

13. The moot question before us is whether the learned Joint District Judge has become functus officio after passing the compromise decree in Title Suit No. 47 of 2003 and become incapable of setting aside the decree passed by him or his predecessor in office by invoking inherent jurisdiction under section 151 of the Cod of Civil Procedure on the ground of fraud. 

14. In the case of Md. Shahidur Rahman Majumder alias Md. Shahidullah Majumder and others vs Sabirunnesa and others, 16 BLD (AD) 50, 1 BLC (AD) 43, their Lordships have found that the learned Assistant Judge set aside the final decree passed in a partition suit on the basis of the report of the Advocate Commissioner by invoking his jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, therefore, held that other remedies such as an appeal is provided by the Code of Civil Procedure; and when there is specific provision for appeal the Court cannot exercise its inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

15. In the instant case, there is apparent bar under section 96(3) as well as sub-section 12 of section 89A of the code of Civil Procedure against filing of any appeal against any order or decree passed on compromise. As per the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that there are alternative remedies for the aggrieved parties such as filing an appeal or a suit for cancellation of decree against the impugned order. Now, the question arises, in spite of having the aforesaid open alternative avenue in getting remedies against the decree in question, whether the obtaining the decree in question has been manifested. 

21. Although the learned Advocate for the petitioner has assailed the propriety of the impugned order on the ground of absence of jurisdiction of the Court in entertaining the petition under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, he did not utter a single word to refute the allegations of committing fraud by the plaintiff petitioner upon the Court in obtaining the order in question. However, he submits that the commission of fraud can be determined after recording evidence, but there is no scope for recording evidence while disposing of a petition filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Where fraud is ex-facie apparent on record, the Court does not require to record any evidence or wait for seeking any mode of alternative remedy by the aggrieved parties against any order or decree procured by practising fraud upon the Court. The Court should instantly bury the fraud to protect the sanctity of the process of Court. So, the decision of the case of Md. Shahidur Rahnzan Majwnder alias Md. Shalzidullah Majumder and others vs Sabirunnesa and others reported in 16 BLD (AD) 50 : 1 BLC (AD) 43 is found to be of no help to the plaintiff petitioner as unlike that case the commission of fraud and it's Consequence is a point for consideration in the case before us. 

22. We have already found that the cases of Master Abdul Aziz vs Abanin Mohan Mukhed ee, 30 DLR (SC) 221, Government of Bangladesh and another vs MA Khair Bhuiyan, 55 DLR (AD) 76, and Deputy Commissioner Bralunanbaria vs Chat& Mia and others, 30 BLC (AD) 138, as mentioned above have dealt with the question of committing fraud in a proceeding before the Court or Tribunal and it's consequences. Conspectus of the decisions mentioned above lead us to hold that a Court can recall it's own order or decree obtained by practising fraud on it and there is no question of becoming the Court functus Such being the case, we hold that the learned Joint District Judge rightly set-aside the compromise decree passed in the Alternative Dispute Resolution Procedure under section 89A of the Code of Civil Procedure by invoking it's inherent power under section 151 of the Code and thereby restored the Suit to it's original file and number to dispose of the same on merit as well as on contest. Accordingly, we find no merit in the Rule. 

23. In view of the above discussions, we are inclined to hold that the Rule should be discharged. It appears that valuable 20 years have elapsed running against a fraudulent order obtained by the plaintiff petitioner and, as such, we are also inclined to impose cost upon the plaintiff petitioner. 

24. In the result, the Rule is discharged with a cost of Taka 5,000 (five thousand). The stay order passed at the time of issuance of Rule is hereby vacated. The learned Joint District Judge is directed to proceed with the suit in accordance with law subject to payment of the cost in favour of the defendants. Since, long delay already caused by this time the learned Joint District Judge is directed to dispose of the suit without further delay. 

Send a copy of the judgment and order to the Court below for disposal of the suit in accordance with same. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Mozibur Rahman Miah, J. This matter has been referred by the Hon’ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh by his order dated 14.01.2025.

2. At the instance of the defendant nos. 4, 7-10 in Title Suit No. 104 of 2018, this appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30.06.2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Gazipur in the said suit decreeing the same on contest against the defendant nos. 1, 3-5, 7-10 and ex parte against the rest.

3. The precise facts leading to preferring this appeal are:
The predecessor of the present respondent nos. 1(a) to 1(b), Nil Roton Sorkar as plaintiff filed the aforesaid suit seeking following reliefs:
“(ক) কালিয়াকৈর সাব রেজিষ্ট্রি অফিসে রেজিষ্ট্রিকৃত বিগত ৬-৪-১০ ইং তারিখে ৪২৩৩ নং ব্যাপক আম-মোক্তার নামা দলিলটি তঞ্চকতাপূর্ণ, যোগসাজসী, প্রতারণামূলক, ফল বলহীন, কাগজী, অবৈধ দলিল বিধায় দলিলটি এবং উক্ত দলিল হইতে উদ্ভূত বিগত ৩১-৮-১০ ইং তারিখে ১০৮৮০ নং সাব কবলা দলিল, ২৭-৯-১০ ইং তারিখে ১১৬৩৭ নং সাব কবলা দলিল, ২৮-৯-১০ ইং তারিখে ১১৭০৭ নং সাব কবলা দলিল ও ২৪-১১-১০ ইং তারিখে ১৪১৫৮ নং বিগত ১১-১-২০১১ ইং তারিখের ৪৬০ নং আম-মোক্তার নামা দলিল, বিগত ৩১-১২-১২ ইং তারিখের সাফ কবলা দলিল নং ১৬৬২৬ ও বিগত ৮-১-১৩ ইং তারিখে ৩২৬ নং সাব কবলা দলিলগুলি তঞ্চকতাপূর্ণ, যোগসাজসী, প্রতারণামূলক, ফল বলহীন, কাগজী, অবৈধ দলিল বিধায় দলিলগুলি অকার্যকর ও বাদীপক্ষের উপর বাধ্যকর নহে মর্মে বাদীপক্ষের অনুকূলে এক ডিক্রি দিতে,
(ক-১) নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে বাদীপক্ষ ষোল আনা স্বত্বের মালিক মর্মে এক ঘোষণা দিতে,
(খ) মোকদ্দমার যাবতীয় ব্যয় বাদীপক্ষের অনুকূলে এবং বিবাদীপক্ষের প্রতিকূলে ডিক্রি দিয়া সুবিচার করিতে মর্জি হয়।
(গ) বাদীপক্ষ বৈধ প্রকারে ও ন্যায় বিচারে আর যে যে প্রতিকার পাওয়ার হকদার তাহাও ডিক্রি দিয়া সুবিচার করিতে মর্জি হয়।"


4. The case of the plaintiff in short is that, the suit lands in C.S Khatian Nos. 26, 136, 154 and 174 along with other lands originally belonged to one, Gadu Nomodas who died intestate leaving behind his three daughters, namely, (i) Radha Rani Sorkar @ Radhika, (ii) Krishno Moni Sorkar and (iii) Kumudini Sorkar. Then Radha Rani Sorkar died leaving behind two sons, Mohadeb Sorkar and Ponchonondo Sarkar when Krishno Moni Sorkar died leaving behind three sons, namely, Dodhi Ram Sorkar, Ponchonondo Sorkar and Nil Roton Sorkar (the plaintiff-predecessor of respondent nos. 1(a)-1(b)). Then Kumudini Sarker died leaving behind one son and four daughters, namely, Monoranjan Sarker (son), Chandraboli Sarker @ Aamodini Sarker, Golapi Rani Sarker, Hiramoti Sarker and Vongorani Sarker (daughters). Subsequently, the lands in C.S Khatain were recorded in S.A Khatian Nos. 73, 300, 347, 326 and 318 in the name of Mohadeb Sorkar, Ponchonondo Sorkar, Dodhi Ram Sorkar, Ponchonondo Sorkar, Nil Roton Sorkar and Monoranjan Sorkar. Thereafter, R.S Khatian being R.S Khatian Nos. 118, 119, 121, 122, 124 and 125 was prepared in the name of Krishno Moni Sorkar and Kumudini Sorkar as of life-interest. However, after the death of the three daughters of Gadu Nomodas, their above mentioned 6(six) sons became the owner of the suit land in equal shares which is 147.50 decimals of land each and had been in possession of the same. Thereafter, Monoranjan Sarkar, the only son of Kumudini Sarkar while being the owner of 147.50 decimals of land by way of inheritance along with some other lands by way of purchase, sold out 100 decimals of land on 24.03.1991 vide deed no. 164 and 155.50 decimals of land on 04.11.1991 vide deed no. 6174 to the plaintiff, Nil Roton Sorkar and then the plaintiff became the owner of 147.50 decimals of land by way of inheritance and 255.50 decimals of land by way of purchase from Monoranjan Sorkar. It has further been stated that, the deed of power of attorney being no. 4233 dated 06.04.2010 in relation to selling the suit land executed by the defendant no. 2, Amudini Sorkar @ Chondraboli Sorkar in favour of the defendant no. 1, Toruni Sorkar and all the following sale deeds and transactions arising out of the aforesaid power of attorney no. 4233 and sale deed no. 10880 dated 31.08.2010 by which defendant no. 1 sold out 25 decimals of land to Md. Azizur Rahman, sale deed no. 11637 dated 27.09.2010 by which defendant no. 1 sold out 73.50 decimals of land to Md. Azmot Ali, sale deed no. 11707 dated 28.09.2010 by which defendant no. 1 sold out 25 decimals of land to Hashem Sikdar, sale deed no. 14158 dated 24.11.2010 by which defendant no. 1 sold out 25 decimals of land to Azizur Rahman, sale deed no. 326 dated 08.01.2013 by why defendant no. 5 Hashem Sikder sold his previously purchased 25 decimals of land to Abdul Hamid Dewan are all null and void. It has also been stated in the plaint that the power of attorney being no. 460 dated 11.01.2011 in relation to selling the suit land executed by the defendant no. 2, Amudini Sorkar @ Chondraboli Sorkar in favour of the defendant no. 1, Toruni Sorkar comprising a total area of 194 decimal of lands vide sale deed no. 16626 dated 31.12.2012 by which the defendant no. 1 sold out 100 decimals of lands to Abdul Hamid Dewan are also null and void and hence the suit.

5. On the other hand, the defendant no. 1, Toruni Sorkar independently and defendant nos. 4 and 5 jointly filed their written statements contending inter alia that the suit lands were originally owned by Gadu Nomodas who died intestate leaving 739 decimals of land to be enjoyed by his three daughters, Radha Rani Sorkar @ Radhika, Krishno Moni Sorkar and Kumudini Sorkar who got 246.333 decimals of lands each and accordingly, R.S Khatain nos. 118, 121, 122, 124 and 125 were prepared in the name of Krishno Moni Sorkar and Kumudini Sorkar having eight anna share each as Radha Rani Sorkar died unmarried. The only son of Kumudini Sorkar that is, Monoranjan Sorkar left the country for India around 40-42 years back and never came back to Bangladesh and he is not the citizen of Bangladesh and thus Kumudini Sorkar died leaving behind her only living daughters Chondraboli Sorkar @ Amudini Sorkar and other three daughters. However, Chondraboli Sorkar @ Amudini Sorkar upon inheriting her mother’s property executed a registered power of attorney being no. 4233 in favour of Toruni Sorkar, the defendant no. 1 on 06.04.2010 and transferred 147 decimals of land to the defendant no. 1. Then vide power of attorney no. 4233, the defendant no. 1, Toruni Sorkar executed a sale deed being no. 11637 dated 23.09.2010 by which he sold out 73.50 decimals of land to one, Md. Azmot Ali. Then by sale deed being no. 11707 dated 28.09.2010 the defendant no. 1 sold out 25 decimals of land to Hashem Sikder. Thereafter, by sale deed being no. 14158 dated 24.11.2010, the defendant no. 1 sold out 25 decimals of land to Azizur Rahman who all are now in possession of their purchased lands. The plaintiff has no title whatsoever in the suit land and hence the suit is liable to be dismissed.

6. The defendant nos. 4 and 5 through jointly contested the suit but they mainly adopted the case of the defendant no. 1 adding that Monoranjan Sarker, son of Kumudini Sorkar left Bangladesh for India around 42-43 years ago and thus he is not a citizen of Bangladesh and never came back to Bangladesh and as a result, at the death of Kumudini Sorkar, her three daughters Horimoti Sorkar, Golapi Sorkar and Chondraboli Sorkar @ Amudini Sorkar inherited Kumudini’s total lands. Then Horimoti Sorkar being the owner of 147.16 decimals of lands, later died leaving behind her only daughter, Jostna Sorkar. Then Golapi Sorkar being the owner of 147.16 decimals of lands died leaving behind her only daughter Jostna Sorkar who died without leaving any successor and hence her other sister/cousin, Jostna Sorkar and aunt, Chondraboli Sorkar @ Amudini Sorkar became the owners of half of 147.16 decimals of lands i.e. 73.58 decimals of land each and in this way, Chondraboli Sorkar @ Amudini Sorkar became the owner of 220.74 decimals of land in the suit land and she then on 06.04.2010 executed and registered a power of attorney being no. 4233 in favour of the defendant no. 1, Toruni Sorkar for transferring 147.50 decimals of land. The defendant no. 1 on 23.09.2010 sold out 73.50 decimals of land to one, Md. Azmot Ali and by sale deed no. 11707, he also sold out 25 decimals of land to one, Hashem Sikder and by sale deed no. 14158 dated 24.11.2010 defendant no. 1 also sold out 25 decimals of land to one, Azizur Rahman who all are now in possession of their purchased lands. Thus Azmot Ali, the defendant no. 4 has been paying taxes of the suit land of 73.50 decimals of land upon mutating his name vide Mutation Case No. 265/11-12. It has also been stated that, Chondraboli Sorkar @ Amudini Sorkar executed another power of attorney being no. 460 dated 11.01.2011 in relation to transferring the suit land in favour of the defendant no. 1, Toruni Sorkar and being empowered by the aforesaid power of attorney, the defendant no. 1, Toruni Sorkar executed a sale deed no. 16626 dated 31.12.2012 selling 100 decimals of land to one, Abdul Hamid Dewan, the father of the defendant nos. 7-10. Then one, Abdul Hamid Dewan also purchased 25 decimals of land on 08.01.2013 sale deed no. 326 from Hasem Sikdar, while defendant no. 5 purchased through sale deed dated 28.09.2010 from defendant no. 1, Toruni Sorkar. Thus Abdul Hamid Dewan, the father of the defendant nos. 7-10 became the owner of 125 decimals of suit land by way of purchase and after his death, his one son and three daughters were substituted as defendant nos. 7, 8, 9 and 10. It has finally been stated that on 17.04.2019 defendant nos. 7, 8, 9 and 10 adopted the written statements submitted by the defendant nos. 4 and 5 as of their own and finally prayed for dismissing the suit.

7. The learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Gazipur in order to dispose of the suit framed as many as 6(six) different issues. During the course of trial, the plaintiff examined 3(three) witnesses and produced documents which were marked as exhibit nos. 1-10 series. While the contesting defendants examined 2 (two) witnesses and produced several documents which were also marked as exhibit nos. ‘ka’- ‘tha’ (L-W). However, after conclusion of trial, the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Gazipur decreed the suit on contest against the defendant nos. 1, 3-5 and 7-10 and ex parte against the rest by his judgment and decree dated 30.06.2019.

8. It is at that stage, the defendant no. 4 and 7-10 as appellants prepared the instant appeal.

9. Mr. Abdus Salam Mamun, the learned senior counsel along with Mr. Md. Mosabbir Hasan Bhuiyan, the learned counsel appearing for the defendant nos. 4, 7-10-appellants upon taking us through the impugned judgment and decree and that of the memorandum of appeal at the very outset submits that the plaintiff did not acquire the property with regard to 255.50 decimals of land by virtue of two sale deeds dated 04.11.1991 and 24.03.1991 respectively, because it has been asserted by the defendants that the vendor of those deeds, Monoranjan Sarker left the country 40-42 years back having no scope to transfer the property by him.

10. To supplement the said submission, the learned counsel contends that since the plaintiff has failed to produce the original copy of two sale deeds and mark those as exhibits, so in absence of any document, no title has accrued to the plaintiff in respect of 255.50 decimals of land and therefore, he has no locus standi to file the suit and proceed with the same.

11. Insofar as regards to 147.50 decimals of land, the claim of the plaintiff as of the heir of Gadu Nomodas, the defendants have got no objection or dispute, the learned counsel further adds.

12. The learned counsel also contends that since R.S record was prepared in the name of Krishnomoni Sarker as well as Kumudini Sarker in 441 decimals of land each, so until and unless, that very R.S record is challenged and cancelled, the plaintiff cannot claim to have acquired any right, title and interest in the suit property.

13. The learned counsel next submits that the present defendants have acquired the suit property by virtue of several sale deeds dated 31.08.2010, 27.09.2010, 28.09.2010, 24.11.2010, 31.12.2012 and 08.01.2013 totaling 273.50 decimals of land and soon after purchasing the said property, the defendants got their respective name mutated in the khatian and accordingly paid rent (khazna) and therefore, they acquired indefeasible title and possession over the suit property while the plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the suit property and therefore, mere filing a suit for declaration of title and challenging those deeds claiming to be inoperative cannot be sustained.

14. The learned counsel by referring to the written statement in particular, paragraph no. gha, also contends that in that paragraph, the defendants have clearly asserted that Monoranjan Sarker, son of Kumudini Sarker left this country 42-43 years back and the said facts have clearly been asserted by the D.W-1 in his testimony having no scope to get any property by the plaintiff, Nil Roton Sarkar from Monoranjan Sarker and therefore, the claim of the plaintiff to get 255.50 decimals of land clearly falls through.

15. The learned counsel further contends that though the plaintiff has produced a certified copy of the sale deed dated 24.03.1991 but since that sale deed has not been marked any exhibit, so through that sale deed, the plaintiff has not acquired any title over that purchased land. In that regard, the learned counsel placed his reliance in the decision reported in 41 DLR (AD) 97 as well as 47 DLR (AD) 45 and submits that in those decisions, it has been settled that if any secondary evidence has to be taken into evidence, the scribe or the attesting witness to the said deed has to be produced before the court to prove the genuineness of such document but in the instant case, though the certified copy of the sale deed has been produced which is a secondary evidence but fact remains, the said deed has not been proved by any scribe or attesting witness.

16. The learned counsel then submits that while producing any secondary evidence, the plaintiff must explain why the original document could not be produced, but there has been nothing to that effect in the entire plaint leaving the claim of acquiring title over 255.50 decimals of land by the plaintiff disproved.

17. In regard to the validity of acquiring ownership over the suit property, the learned counsel then placed his reliance to the decision reported in 15 MLR (AD) 17 and submits that it is the plaintiff who is to prove his own case since the plaintiff relied upon two sale deeds claimed to have purchased from one, Monoranjan Sarker but he has failed to prove acquiring ownership by alleged purchase so he cannot get any title in the suit property and therefore, that very decision is squarely applicable in the case of the plaintiff.

18. When we pose a question to the learned counsel for the appellant that in spite of R.S record is prepared in the name of Krishnomoni Sarker and Kumudini Sarker and the vendor of the defendants claimed to have acquired the property from the daughter of Kumudini Sarker named, Chandraboli Sarker alias Amodini Sarker, when it is the provision so have been provided in the Dayabhaga School of inheritance, authored by Mulla’s Hindu Law that no daughter will inherit the property left by her father or grandfather, the learned counsel then contends that since R.S record has still been subsisting in the name of the mother of Chandraboli Sarker so there has been no scope for Nil Roton Sarkar to acquire the property from Monoranjan Sarker.

19. The learned counsel lastly contends that since the property has been acquired by the predecessor of the defendants that is, Chandraboli Sarker as the descendent of Gadu Nomodas so said Chandraboli Sarker has rightly inherited the property and in that regard, the learned counsel cited a decision of the Appellate Division passed in Civil Appeal No. 55 of 2003 and submits that the ratio settled therein is applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case and finally prays for allowing the appeal on setting aside the impugned judgment and decree. 

20. On the contrary, Mr. Mukunda Chandra Debnath along with Mr. Palash Kanti Das, the learned counsels appearing for the respondent no. 1(a) to 1(b) very robustly opposes the contention taken by the learned counsel for the appellants and submits that since the appellants as defendants in their entire written statement did not challenge the propriety of the purchase deed dated 04.11.1991 and 24.03.1991 through which the plaintiff-respondents got 255.50 decimals of land in total from Monoranjan Sarker, so there has been no occasion on the part of the defendants to assail the validity of the deeds for the first time before this court. In that regard, the learned counsel has placed his reliance in the decision reported in 53 DLR (AD) 45 and takes us through paragraphs 6 and 8 thereof and submits that in those paragraphs it has been clearly held that “Since specific assertion has not denied specifically either in written statements or in evidence, the court is not inclined to permit the defendants to raise such a question at this stage.” and therefore, the decision reported in 47 DLR (AD) 45 relied upon by the learned counsel for the appellants cannot be sustained in the facts and circumstances of the instant case.

21. The learned counsel further contends that the cardinal point to be adjudicated in the instant appeal is, whether Chandraboli Sarker can inherit the property left by her maternal-grandfather, Gadu Nomodas and if Chandraboli Sarker does not acquire any property left by Gadu Nomodas then she had no saleable right to transfer any property by any means in favour of the predecessor of the defendants-appellants. In that regard, the learned counsel by referring to paragraph no. 88 titled “order of succession among sapindas” according to Dayabhaga or Bengal School provided in Chapter VII of Mulla’s “Hindu Law” submits that the first ‘sapinda’ will be “son” then “grandson” and thereafter, “great-grandson” so under that very provision of order of succession in “Dayabhaga School” followed by the Hindu in Bangladesh, there has been no scope for Chandraboli Sarker to inherit any property left by Gadu Nomodas let alone she reserved any right to transfer property to the defendants.

22. When we pose a question to the learned counsel with regard to the judgment so relied upon by the defendants-appellants passed in Civil Appeal No. 55 of 2003 dated 11.12.2022, the learned counsel then takes us through page no. 15 of the said judgment and submits that in that decision, the predecessor of the plaintiff “Rukkhini Dashi” got the property by virtue of registered patta dated 24 Boishakh 1311 B.S and that property was regarded as stridhana property and the plaintiff namely, Elokeshi Mondal claimed the said stridhana property as of grand-daughter of that “Rukkhini Dashi” and therefore, the facts so have been described in the cited decision is explicitly distinguishable with the facts and circumstances of the instant case as in the instant case, no stridhana property has been claimed by the predecessor of the defendants, Chandraboli Sarker rather Chandraboli Sarker claimed to have acquired the property as one of the descendents of Gadu Nomodas which is totally contrary to the provision as has been provided in paragraph no. 88 of Chapter VII of Mulla’s Hindu Law (supra) and therefore, there had been no scope on the part of the Chandraboli Sarker either to give any power of attorney to anybody else let alone to transfer the suit property to the defendants by virtue of sale deeds which have been called in question in the suit.

23. The learned counsel further submits that though the plaintiff has produced the certified copy of the sale deed dated 24.03.1991 through which 100 decimals of land has been transferred by Monoranjan Sarker in favour of plaintiff, Nil Roton Sarkar but the court witness no. 1 (C.W-1) found the khatian number stated therein as 135 in place of 136, however he clearly found nexus among the khatian so described in the plaint with that of the khatian mentioned in the volume called balamboi (h¡m¡jhC) and as the defendants declined to cross-examine the said C.W-1 so it alternatively proves that the plaintiff has rightly acquired title and possession over the suit land by two sale deeds dated 04.11.1991 and 24.03.1991. With those submissions, the learned counsel finally prays for dismissing the appeal by affirming the judgment and decree passed by the learned Judge of the trial court.

24. Be that as it may, we have considered the submission so advanced by the learned senior counsel for the appellants and that of the learned counsel for the respondent no. 1(a) to 1(b).

25. The crux of the dispute among the parties is, whether the predecessor of the defendants, Chandraboli Sarker has got any saleable right to transfer the property measuring an area of 273.50 decimals of land in favour of the defendants or not.

26. To dwell on that cardinal point, we have very meticulously gone through the provision so have been provided in Hindu Law authored by D.F Mulla and chapter VII thereof where paragraph no. 88 is very much pertinent in adjudicating the instant appeal.

27. There has been no gainsaying the fact that the order of succession among ‘sapindas’ provided in paragraph no. 88 of that Chapter, it has clearly been stipulated that “son” then “grandson” and finally “greatgrandson” will take precedence in inheriting the property left by their predecessor. So under no circumstances, can the daughter’s daughter of Gadu Nomodas, namely, Chandrabati Sarker that is, the predecessor of the defendants can get the property left by their maternal grandfather, Gadu Nomodas. For argument’s sake, since R.S record was prepared in the name of the mother of Chandraboli Sarker, Kumudini Sarker in 441 decimals of land each yet as per order of succession among ‘sapindas’ provided in paragraph no. 88, we don’t find that, Chandraboli Sarker ever acquired any property as heir of Kumudini Sarker rather her son, Monoranjan Sarker acquired total quantum of land that is, 441 decimals of land. In such a view of the matter, in spite of preparation of R.S record in the name of the predecessor of both Monoranjan Sarker and Chandraboli Sarker that is, Kumudini Sarker still as per the Dayabhaga School of inheritance, Chandraboli Sarker can never acquire any property from her mother as her descendent.

28. Another pertinent point that has been cropped up during the course of hearing as to whether the plaintiff acquired title and possession over 255.50 decimals of land by virtue of two sale deeds. Since the onus squarely lies upon the defendants to prove that at the time of transfer by those two sale deeds, Monoranjan Sarker was not present in this country or in other words, he was not the citizen of this country, as has been asserted by them in their written statement saying that, Monoranjan Sarker left the country 42-43 years back, but it remained disproved as not a scrap of document has been produced by the defendant to prove that fact. Rather, it alternatively proves, the plaintiff acquired 255.50 decimals of land through two sale deeds and since the defendants did not dispute with regard to acquiring rest 147.50 decimals of land as of descendent of Gadu Nomodas, so the plaintiff has perfectly acquired 403.00 decimals of land in total and hence, the plaintiff has rightly challenged the sale deeds so have been made in favour of the defendants by the attorney of Chandraboli Sarker. Because, if those sale deeds remain in operation, it will certainly cast cloud over the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land he purchased from Monoranjan Sarker when it has also been proved, Chandraboli Sarker did not acquire any property left by Gadu Nomodas. Given the above perspective, the plaintiff has rightly filed the suit challenging the propriety of the sale deeds apart from praying for declaration of title in the entire suit properties.

29. Further, on going through the decision passed in Civil Appeal No. 55 of 2003 by the Appellate Division on which the learned counsel for the defendants has hugely placed their reliance, we have thus very meticulously gone through it, and find that in the said decision, whether the stridhana property will be inherited by the successor of their predecessor or not has been decided. But under no circumstances, can the said decision bears any nexus with the facts and circumstances of the case in hand. Because, in the instant case, the plaintiff has challenged the propriety of 6(six) sale deeds made through power of attornies as well as title in the suit property and it is admitted position that, the plaintiff of the said cited decision claimed stridhana property as a heirs of her grandmother which was upheld by the Appellate Division and what is stridhana property has clearly been described at page no. 18 and that of the case of the plaintiff at page no. 15. So it is abundantly clear that the decision upon which the learned counsel put his reliance has got no relevance with the facts and circumstances of the instant case and thus totally inapplicable here as the plaintiff of the instant case has never claimed stridhana property as any heir of his predecessor.

30. Then again, though the learned counsel for the appellant cited a decision with regard to the admissibility of secondary evidence but we don’t find the said decision is applicable here as well in view of not disputing the authenticity of the deeds dated 04.11.1991 and 24.03.1991 by the defendant as had the defendants raised such objection, the plaintiff would have surely taken defence with that regard by cross examining the witness of the defendants.

31. Also, we have examined the decision reported in 15 MLR (AD) 17 as well and we are of the view that it is the universal proposition that, the plaintiff has to prove his/her own case without depending on the weakness of the defendant’s case. But the case in hand, the plaintiff has challenged the propriety of 6(six) sale deeds preceded by power of attornies couple with declaration of title in the suit land as made out in the prayer of the plaint. So, plaintiff was duty bound to prove his case on those scores which he has discharged but certainly the plaintiff is not obliged to controvert to what has not been asserted in the written statement by the defendants.

32. Overall, with the above discussion and observation, it has been abundantly proved that the plaintiff has been able to prove his case in line with the plaint so invariably we find the above decision goes in favour of the plaintiff.

33. Regard being had to the above facts and circumstances, we don’t find any illegality or impropriety in the impugned judgment and decree which is liable to be sustained.

34. Resultantly, the appeal is dismissed however without any order as to costs.

Let a copy of this judgment along with the lower court records be transmitted to the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Gazipur forthwith.
